"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03307824": "This study explores the role of carbon labelling in the food sector as a tool to reduce carbon emissions and promote sustainable consumption, focusing specifically on sandwich products including the ham and cheese sandwich. Carbon labelling informs consumers about the carbon emissions associated with a product\u2019s production, distribution, and disposal. Using mixed qualitative and quantitative methodologies, the study investigates consumer perceptions of carbon labelling and its impact on purchasing behavior, while also analyzing carbon emissions within the food industry. \n\nA Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) was conducted to evaluate the carbon footprints of two sandwich recipes: a ham and cheese sandwich and a cheese and mayonnaise sandwich. The LCA results showed that the ham and cheese sandwich has a significantly higher carbon footprint, ranging between 1053 and 1070 g CO2 equivalent, compared to 700 to 750 g CO2 equivalent for the cheese and mayonnaise sandwich. Key contributors to these emissions include ingredient production, packaging, and energy use during manufacturing. Collaboration with a sandwich maker allowed comprehensive data collection and a detailed carbon footprint analysis spanning the entire production process.\n\nSurvey results highlight a disparity between consumer awareness and behavior: while 68.6% of respondents recognize the importance of carbon labelling, only 26.9% report that this influences their purchasing choices. This gap suggests that although consumers express concern about carbon footprints, carbon labelling alone may not strongly drive behavior change.\n\nThe study emphasizes that educating consumers, standardizing carbon labelling practices, and modifying sandwich recipes\u2014such as potentially reformulating the ham and cheese sandwich\u2014could enhance the effectiveness of carbon labelling. Such measures could encourage greener consumption patterns and contribute to lowering the carbon footprints of food products, including the high-impact ham and cheese sandwich, thereby supporting the food industry\u2019s goal of a sustainable, low-carbon future.",

The hot and humid climate in the region renders mechanical weed control inefficient, prompting farmers to rely on herbicides. However, the impact of herbicides, particularly glyphosate, on guarana seed development and quality has been largely unknown. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of glyphosate on guarana seedling growth, development, and quality to better inform integrated weed management practices.\n\nThe experiment involved applying various glyphosate doses\u20140, 126, 252, 540, 1080, 2160, and 3240 g a.e. ha<sup>\u22121</sup>\u2014over a 60-day period, with two application events. Key parameters assessed included biometrics, seedling development, anthracnose incidence, and visual injury symptoms. Results indicated that glyphosate caused injury symptoms in guarana seedlings at all tested doses, although lower doses did not significantly interfere with seedling growth or development. Notably, a positive correlation was observed between glyphosate dose and the severity of anthracnose, a common fungal disease affecting guarana seeds and seedlings.\n\nThese findings suggest that while glyphosate can induce some level of injury to guarana seedlings and potentially influence seed quality through increased anthracnose severity, careful and appropriate application of glyphosate doses may allow its use as an effective component of integrated weed management strategies in guarana seed production. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03490235": "This case report discusses a rare late complication occurring 8 years after inguinal hernia repair using a polypropylene plug mesh. Mesh infection is a known short-term complication following hernia repair, but it seldom leads to the development of an ileocutaneous fistula. The patient, a 67-year-old male, initially underwent right inguinal hernia repair with a polypropylene plug. Years later, he presented with skin ulceration and pus in the right groin, and was eventually diagnosed with an enterocutaneous fistula.\n\nLaparoscopic exploration revealed that the ileum near the fistula was closely adherent to the abdominal wall. During surgery, after careful separation of the bowel loop, a 2 \u00d7 3 cm defect was identified on the ileal surface. Further laparotomy showed that the polypropylene plug mesh was embedded inside the ileum. The plug was completely removed, and an ileum side-to-side anastomosis was performed to restore bowel integrity. The patient recovered well, being discharged two weeks post-operation, and six-month follow-up showed complete wound healing without hernia recurrence.\n\nThis case highlights the importance of considering late-onset ileocutaneous fistula as a differential diagnosis in patients presenting with inflammation or abscess at the site of prior hernia repair with polypropylene plug mesh. The report emphasizes that laparoscopic exploration should be prioritized for suspected intestinal fistulas following such repairs. Additionally, it underlines the necessity of customizing the approach to mesh removal based on laparoscopic findings, particularly when dealing with complications involving polypropylene plug mesh integration into adjacent bowel tissue.\n\nIn conclusion, while polypropylene plug mesh is widely used for inguinal hernia repair, clinicians should remain alert to rare but serious late complications like ileocutaneous fistula formation and plan surgical interventions accordingly.",

Moreover, eucalyptus plantations established in savannahs far from natural forests can function as catalysts for the natural regeneration of native species, promoting recovery processes that would not occur without them. The sedimentation technique was employed for sample examination. Results showed Giardia lamblia (71.1%) as the dominant protozoan parasite and Ascaris lumbricoides (15.6%) as the common helminth parasite. Statistical analysis (T-test, p<0.05) revealed significant differences in contamination rates among vegetable types. The study found no direct relationship between the percentage of parasite contamination on fresh vegetables in markets and the rate of intestinal parasitic infections in nearby hospitals. This difference is attributed to the combined inhibitory effects of rhamnogalacturonans (RG-I and RG-II), yeast-derived mannoproteins, and total polyphenols present in red wines. Arabinogalactans show no impact on KHT crystallization, whereas rhamnogalacturonans display a concentration-dependent effect: accelerating KHT crystal appearance at low concentrations and slowing it at high concentrations. This behavior, especially pronounced for RG-II fractions, aligns with crystallization theory, which suggests RG-I has minimal effect on KHT nucleation while RG-II enhances nucleation but both inhibit crystal growth by adsorbing onto growth sites, as confirmed by single crystal experiments.\n\nRed wines are more challenging to stabilize against KHT crystallization by cooling due to their higher RG-II and total polyphenol content. Low RG-II levels in white wines accelerate KHT crystal appearance, whereas high RG-II levels in red wines slow it, thereby intensifying inhibition caused by total polyphenols. Additionally, mannoproteins extracted from yeast cell walls strongly inhibit KHT crystallization more than those naturally present in wine, though their efficacy decreases at lower temperatures.\n\nOverall, potassium hydrogen tartrate crystallization in wines is modulated by specific macromolecules, with red wines showing greater natural inhibition due to their unique composition.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03310802": "Licorice, commonly found as a licorice-type candy and widely used as a flavoring additive in tea, tobacco, and sweets, is one of the oldest medicinal herbs, containing up to 300 active compounds. Its main active constituent is glycyrrhizin, a prodrug that is metabolized in the intestines to 3\u03b2-monoglucuronyl-18\u03b2-glycyrrhetinic acid (3MGA) and 18\u03b2-glycyrrhetinic acid (GA). Despite licorice-type candy\u2019s reported health benefits, these metabolites inhibit the enzyme 11\u03b2-hydrogenase type II (11\u03b2-HSD2), which normally converts cortisol to inactive cortisone. This inhibition leads to elevated cortisol levels that activate mineralocorticoid receptors, resulting in apparent mineralocorticoid excess in the kidneys and increased systemic vascular resistance.\n\nExcessive licorice consumption, including through licorice-type candy, can cause sodium retention (hypernatremia), potassium loss (hypokalemia), and increased fluid volume. Such disturbances may lead to serious, potentially life-threatening complications, particularly in individuals with pre-existing cardiovascular conditions. Two recent meta-analyses encompassing 18 and 26 studies respectively have shown that licorice intake, including licorice-type candy consumption, is associated with statistically significant increases in blood pressure\u2014specifically, systolic pressure rising by an average of 5.45 mmHg, and diastolic pressure increasing by 3.19 and 1.74 mmHg.\n\nThis review highlights the dual nature of licorice-type candy and licorice-based products, balancing recognized health benefits against their risk of adverse cardiovascular effects linked to increased blood pressure and mineralocorticoid activity. Understanding licorice\u2019s molecular effects, particularly those of its metabolites within the human body, is crucial to delineating safe consumption boundaries. Accordingly, while licorice-type candy remains a popular treat and medicinal ingredient, caution is warranted regarding its intake to avoid harmful cardiovascular outcomes.",

Contaminated production equipment often contains food product contact surfaces that are difficult to clean and disinfect due to inaccessible parts. Factors such as the temperature, position, and material of these food product contact surfaces contribute significantly to bacterial contamination within plants. Current investigations have advanced the understanding of how and when food items become contaminated during production, yet major challenges remain, particularly the adherence of L. monocytogenes to food product contact surfaces and its ability to form biofilms. In the biofilm state, bacteria display increased resistance to stress factors typically employed for decontamination of food product contact surfaces. Effective control of L. monocytogenes in food production is achievable mainly through integrated programs that align with Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) and Good Hygiene Practice (GHP) systems, focusing heavily on hygiene and sanitation of food product contact surfaces. Control measures aimed at reducing L. monocytogenes contamination involve strict hygiene procedures targeting food product contact surfaces and the use of appropriate technological interventions during production. Ultimately, maintaining clean and properly treated food product contact surfaces is essential for minimizing bacterial contamination in finished food products and ensuring consumer safety.",

The plasma device employed a top electrode with multiple pins to generate corona discharge of electrons for effective starch modification. Arrowroot starch samples (10 g) were exposed to cold plasma at three input voltages (190, 210, 230 V) for durations ranging from 5 to 15 minutes. The study evaluated various properties of the plasma-treated arrowroot starch, including intrinsic viscosity average molecular weight (MWv), powder flow properties (bulk and tapped density, Hausner's ratio, Carr's index), functional characteristics (water and oil binding capacity, pH, gel hydration, turbidity), rheological behavior (pasting and steady shear flow), as well as thermal (DSC) and structural (FTIR, XRD, SEM) properties.\n\nResults showed that cold plasma treatment increased the MWv of arrowroot starch, indicating cross-linking within the starch molecules. This cross-linking was also evidenced by an increase in peak viscosity of the starch pastes by 4.33% to 11.98%. The steady shear viscosity at a shear rate of 50 s\u207b\u00b9 increased significantly (15.44% to 223.83%) compared to untreated arrowroot starch. Structural analysis via SEM revealed surface etching and the inclusion of acidic and hydrophilic functional groups, which contributed to a decrease in pH of arrowroot starch from 5.41 \u00b1 0.03 to 4.01 \u00b1 0.01. Functional properties improved with a 22.5% rise in water binding capacity and an 8.46% increase in oil binding for the highest voltage and treatment time (230 V, 15 min). Additionally, swelling volume increased by 50%, solubility index rose by 240%, while paste turbidity decreased, indicating a clearer starch paste.\n\nXRD and DSC analysis revealed an increase in crystallinity percentage and gelatinization enthalpy, demonstrating enhanced thermal stability of plasma-treated arrowroot starch due to cross-linking. Reducing wheel wear, including the prevention of crumbling tread surfaces, is crucial for lowering operating costs in railway transport. In Thailand, the cultivation area of peach palm fruit has been steadily increasing since its introduction for fruit production. Recently, leaf spot disease symptoms, characterized by small brown spots expanding into irregular lesions with dark margins, were observed on peach palm fruit seedlings in commercial nurseries located in Phetchaburi Province, southern Thailand. To identify the causal agents of this disease affecting peach palm fruit, ten fungal isolates were collected from symptomatic leaves and tested for pathogenicity, confirming their role in causing the disease.\n\nMorphological and molecular analyses identified five isolates as <i>Colletotrichum fructicola</i> (BGC02.2, BGC03) and <i>C. theobromicola</i> (BGC01, BGC02.1, BGC04), and the other five as <i>Fusarium pernambucanum</i> (BGF01, BGF02, BGF03, BGF04.1, BGF04.2). Phylogenetic analysis for <i>Colletotrichum</i> species was conducted based on multiple genetic regions including <i>act</i>, <i>cal</i>, <i>gapdh</i>, ITS, and <i>tub2</i>, while for <i>Fusarium</i> species, the genes <i>cal</i>, <i>rpb2</i>, and <i>tef1-\u03b1</i> were analyzed.\n\nIn vitro fungicide sensitivity assays showed that the <i>Colletotrichum</i> species affecting peach palm fruit were most sensitive to carbendazim, mancozeb, and prochloraz. Meanwhile, <i>Fusarium pernambucanum</i> was effectively inhibited by mancozeb and prochloraz. This research marks the first report of <i>C. fructicola</i>, <i>C. theobromicola</i>, and <i>F. pernambucanum</i> causing leaf spot disease on peach palm fruit in Thailand. These findings provide important insights for developing effective disease management strategies to sustain peach palm fruit cultivation in the region.",

The findings highlight that trans fatty acids adversely affect serum lipid profiles and are metabolically distinct from natural cis fatty acid isomers.\n\nOverall, the soft margarine, being high in linoleate and free from trans fatty acids, demonstrated beneficial effects on lowering total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B, distinguishing it favorably from both hard margarine and butter-based diets. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_00005289": "This study investigates the molecular and biochemical basis of postharvest seed coat darkening in mature cranberry bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) varieties. Darkening during storage reduces market value, and this trait is linked to the presence and oxidation of proanthocyanidins in the seed coat. Mature cranberry bean lines that do not exhibit postharvest darkening tend to lack proanthocyanidins, although the reasons for this deficiency were previously unclear.\n\nIn this research, proanthocyanidin levels increased as mature cranberry bean plants developed in a darkening-susceptible recombinant inbred line (RIL), while these compounds were absent in the non-darkening RIL. RNA sequencing analysis of the seed coat transcriptome in mature cranberry bean RILs revealed 1,336 genes differentially expressed between darkening and non-darkening types. Notably, structural and regulatory genes involved in proanthocyanidin biosynthesis were upregulated in darkening-susceptible mature cranberry bean seed coats.\n\nPrincipal component analysis identified strong correlations between proanthocyanidin accumulation and transcript levels of two genes of unknown function, along with three key biosynthetic genes: FLAVANONE 3-HYDROXYLASE 1, DIHYDROFLAVONOL 4-REDUCTASE 1, and ANTHOCYANIDIN REDUCTASE 1 (PvANR1) in mature cranberry bean seed coats. Biochemical assays showed that recombinant PvANR1 from mature cranberry bean was NADPH-dependent and converted the substrate cyanidin into epicatechin and catechin, proanthocyanidin building blocks. High levels of cyanidin inhibited this enzymatic activity.\n\nThe results indicate that proanthocyanidin accumulation, driven by the upregulation of biosynthesis genes including PvANR1 during maturation, is critical for postharvest seed coat darkening in mature cranberry bean. This study provides insight into the metabolic and genetic factors underlying seed coat darkening and proanthocyanidin biosynthesis in mature cranberry bean, highlighting PvANR1\u2019s role in converting cyanidin to key proanthocyanidin monomers necessary for this trait.",

Specifically, crystallisation in frozen food can be influenced by the application of magnetic, electric, and electromagnetic fields during freezing. Static magnetic fields (SMF) may affect the crystallisation process in frozen food; however, their effectiveness remains under debate within scientific literature. On the other hand, static electric fields (SEF) have demonstrated significant impact on crystallisation in frozen food, supported both by experimental evidence and theoretical understanding. Oscillating magnetic fields generate oscillating electric fields, which are expected to interact with water crystallisation in frozen food. Furthermore, oscillating electromagnetic fields can perturb or disrupt hydrogen bonds in water, potentially increasing supercooling levels and promoting the formation of numerous fine ice crystals in frozen food. The frequency of these fields appears to influence these effects, although the exact relationships require further study. This review highlights the fundamental mechanisms of freezing under magnetic, electric, and electromagnetic fields and explores their applicability and potential benefits in frozen food processing. CTX levels and toxin profiles varied among fish species and between collection sites. N2a assay results also indicated the presence of other CTX-like toxins or sodium channel activators in I-Kiribati fish specimens. Addressing this gap, the present study focused on sequencing the complete mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) of the endangered smooth-hound species <i>Mustelus schmitti</i>, also known as the narrownose smooth-hound shark. The obtained mitochondrial genome was 16,764 base pairs long and contained the typical 13 protein-coding genes, 22 tRNAs, two ribosomal RNAs (12S and 16S), and a large <i>D-loop</i> region, exhibiting a genomic organization consistent with other members of the smooth-hound genus <i>Mustelus</i>.\n\nTo explore phylogenetic relationships within the smooth-hound genus and the broader Triakidae family, the study conducted a phylogenetic analysis using the Maximum Likelihood method. The results supported the monophyly of the Triakidae family, clustering all smooth-hound genus species into a well-defined topology group. However, polyphyletic patterns emerged in certain species, including <i>Galeorhinus galeus</i>, <i>Hemiatrakis japanica</i>, and two species from the genus <i>Triakis</i> (<i>Triakis megalopterus</i> and <i>Triakis semifasciata</i>), suggesting complex evolutionary relationships within some smooth-hound genus members.\n\nIn summary, this study advances the genetic understanding of the endangered smooth-hound genus by providing a complete mitochondrial genome sequence for <i>Mustelus schmitti</i> and clarifying phylogenetic connections within the Triakidae family. Crop wild relatives (CWRs) of Indian mustard, which are closely related weedy species often neglected because of undesirable alleles affecting yield, hold valuable genetic diversity for enhancing stress tolerance. Key CWRs associated with mustard and cress include Sinapis alba (white mustard), Brassica tournefortii (African mustard), Crambe abyssinica (Abyssinian mustard), Erucastrum gallicum and E. cardaminoides (dogmustards), as well as Lepidium sativum (garden cress). These CWRs have evolved under diverse biotic and abiotic stresses over millennia, leading to the accumulation of resistance traits valuable for B. juncea improvement. This review highlights research on transferring resistance against major diseases like Sclerotinia stem rot (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum), Alternaria blight (Alternaria brassicae), white rust (Albugo candida), and pests such as aphids, along with drought and high-temperature tolerance from mustard and cress CWRs into Indian mustard. Despite the potential, crosses encounter significant pre- and post-fertilization barriers due to ploidy differences, complicating breeding efforts. Advances in -omics technologies, including genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics, offer promising tools to overcome these challenges by identifying stress-related alleles and facilitating marker-assisted selection and gene editing. Utilizing these approaches can accelerate the introgression of resilience traits from mustard and cress wild relatives into B. juncea, thereby enhancing crop stability and productivity under changing environmental conditions. However, the productivity and health of these herring stocks have declined since 1965, and despite recovery-oriented management efforts since 2003, biomass remains low and continues to decrease. One major challenge is that the primary factors driving 4VWX herring productivity remain unresolved, which likely limits the success of current management strategies.\n\nThis study evaluated potential drivers of herring population variability by analyzing 52 time-series data sets encompassing physical, ecological, and anthropogenic influences on the 4VWX herring population. Additionally, environmental factors such as thermal phenology and temperature negatively affected early life stage mortality rates, while egg predation had a positive effect.\n\nImportantly, the findings highlight that the current management approach for 4VWX herring does not adequately consider the early life stage dynamics within the broader ecosystem context. The study emphasizes the need to assess herring population fluctuations and management within the ecosystem and climate change frameworks to improve recovery outcomes. Incorporating ecosystem-based perspectives is essential because these early life stages and their interactions with environmental and ecological factors directly influence adult biomass and overall stock health.\n\nIn summary, a more comprehensive, ecosystem-informed management approach is critical to addressing the unresolved drivers of variability in 4VWX herring populations. Considering ecosystem dynamics, including the effects of temperature, phenology, and predation within climate change contexts, will likely enhance the effectiveness of conservation and sustainable harvesting measures. This ecosystem perspective is broadly relevant not only for 4VWX herring but also for improving fisheries management in other marine systems.",

In contrast, Cu and Al elements and their weaker bonds (Al-Al and Cu-Cu) are more involved in localized shear transformations, which are precursors to plastic deformation. \n\nA critical finding is that yielding in this metallic material is triggered by a substantial structural reconstruction, characterized by the halt of increase in bond lengths and decrease in bond angles of intermediate and stronger bonds. This bond behavior marks the transition from elastic to plastic deformation. After yielding, all elements and bonds become active participants in the plastic deformation process, with the stronger bonds playing a major role in maintaining residual strength and influencing the ultimate fracture strain of the metallic material.\n\nThese insights enhance the understanding of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms in multicomponent metallic materials, particularly metallic glasses, and provide valuable guidance for tailoring their compositions. Notably, when hunting grounds expanded in 1814 (Greenland Sea) and 1817 (Davis Strait), shifts in size distribution followed. Before expansion, 85% of bowhead whales (as estimated from bowhead whale oil yields) in the East Canada-West Greenland stock were sexually mature (>13 m), compared to only 39% in the East Greenland-Svalbard-Barents stock. After expansion, sexually mature proportions declined to 50% and increased to 44%, respectively.\n\nThese findings highlight the significant value of bowhead whale oil yield data in reconstructing historical whaling impacts and whale population dynamics. Understanding these past trends is crucial given that commercial hunting of bowhead whales in the European Arctic has ceased, but the region has since undergone substantial oceanographic and sea ice changes. UC and SR methods showed markedly increased success during the breeding season (84.2\u2013100%) compared to the nonbreeding season (25.0\u201333.3%), emphasizing seasonal influences on collection of polar bear sperm material.\n\nNotably, four males (57% of those undergoing SR) displayed testicular tumors, a factor of concern in polar bear reproductive health. A total of 13 sperm samples (1 EEJ, 9 UC, and 3 SR) were cryopreserved using egg-yolk-based equine extender (EQ) or OptiXcell (OP). Post-thaw assessments indicated a reduction in sperm motility and viability by 20\u201360% and 30\u201365%, respectively, regardless of extender type, highlighting challenges in preserving polar bear sperm material viability after freezing.\n\nOverall, these results provide valuable insights for optimizing polar bear sperm collection and cryopreservation techniques. A precise droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) method was developed to detect and quantify salmon trout (raw) adulteration in Atlantic salmon. The approach uses species-specific primers and probes targeting the single-copy nuclear myoglobin gene of both salmonids, enabling accurate differentiation between Atlantic salmon and salmon trout (raw).\n\nA quantitative formula was established to calculate the mass fraction of salmon trout (raw) in Atlantic salmon based on DNA copy number ratios converted into meat mass fractions through a fixed transfer coefficient. Repeatability and reproducibility were high, with relative standard deviations (RSDs) below 5% for known salmon trout (raw) meat mixtures.\n\nImportantly, the method\u2019s accuracy was unaffected by common food processing treatments such as thermal and freezing processes or the addition of food additives within recommended levels. The ddPCR technique was successfully applied to commercial products, effectively detecting salmon trout (raw) adulteration in both raw and processed Atlantic salmon items. When compared to real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR), the ddPCR assay showed superior stability and accuracy in identifying and quantifying salmon trout (raw) presence.\n\nOverall, this ddPCR-based method offers a highly accurate, sensitive, and practical tool for routine monitoring and quality control to detect salmon trout (raw) adulteration in Atlantic salmon products, supporting food safety and market regulation efforts.",

The system\u2019s maturity stages were referenced and validated using refractometry to measure total soluble solids (TSS) expressed in \u00b0 Brix. Two classifiers were tested: a radial basis function artificial neural network (RBF-ANN) and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS). The RBF-ANN achieved 100% accuracy in classifying the ripeness of sweet orange bell peppers, outperforming the ANFIS model, which achieved 88% accuracy.\n\nAdditionally, the study developed a \u00b0 Brix prediction model with improvements over existing approaches. Specifically, in the darnel plant, methanol modifies wound-induced MAPK signaling, suggesting a distinctive role of methanol as an elicitor-active DAMP in monocot grasses. The authors propose that plants perceive methanol as a signal of self-damage, with methanol acting primarily as a DAMP-like alarm signal in dicots but serving as a stronger elicitor in monocot grasses such as the darnel plant. The study also notes that ethanol, though less well understood in plant stress responses, exhibits effects similar to methanol on signaling to DAMPs and MAMPs.\n\nThus, the research highlights the differential effects of methanol on defense signaling in dicots versus monocots and underscores the importance of methanol in modulating defense responses in the darnel plant Lolium temulentum and other grasses.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03413190": "The Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS) conducted a scientific re-evaluation of the safety of polyglycerol polyricinoleate (PGPR, E 476) as a food additive. Previously, in 1978, the Scientific Committee for Food (SCF) had established an acceptable daily intake (ADI) for polyglycerol polyricinoleate at 7.5 mg/kg body weight (bw) per day. PGPR undergoes hydrolysis in the gut, releasing free polyglycerols, polyricinoleic acid, and ricinoleic acid. Smaller molecules such as di- and triglycerol are absorbed and excreted unchanged via urine, whereas long-chain polyglycerols exhibit limited absorption and are primarily excreted unchanged in feces.\n\nToxicological data indicate that polyglycerol polyricinoleate has low acute oral toxicity. Short-term and subchronic studies show that PGPR is well tolerated even at high doses without adverse effects. There is no concern related to genotoxicity or carcinogenicity of polyglycerol polyricinoleate. However, the available reproductive toxicity study on PGPR was limited and insufficient for deriving a health-based guidance value. Human studies with polyglycerol polyricinoleate reveal no significant adverse effects.\n\nOf particular importance is a 2-year combined chronic toxicity/carcinogenicity study of polyglycerol polyricinoleate, which provided a no observed adverse effect level (NOAEL) of 2,500 mg/kg bw per day\u2014the highest tested dose. Based on these findings, the Panel concluded that the current data justify revising the established ADI for polyglycerol polyricinoleate from 7.5 to 25 mg/kg bw per day. Exposure assessments showed that current and proposed uses of polyglycerol polyricinoleate would not exceed this revised ADI.\n\nConsequently, the Panel recommended updating the EU specifications for polyglycerol polyricinoleate (E 476) to reflect these safety findings. In summary, the re-evaluation supports the safety of polyglycerol polyricinoleate at the proposed higher intake level, ensuring its continued safe use as a food additive.",

Further structural elucidation by Fourier Transform Infra-Red Spectroscopy validated the characteristic spectral bands of fructan in the AFF fractions. The prebiotic activity of these inulin-derived fructose-based fructan fractions was tested in vitro using Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus strains. These advantages include rapid and volumetric heating, higher energy efficiency\u2014facilitating the use of electricity from sustainable sources\u2014and reduced sensory and quality loss during pasteurization by heating. In fruit products with low pH levels that inhibit harmful microorganism growth, pasteurization by heating primarily targets heat-resistant enzymes such as peroxidase, polyphenol oxidase, and pectin methylesterase to ensure product safety and quality. Simulation results provided insights into electric field distribution, temperature profiles during pasteurization by heating, and power losses due to reflection. Using electromagnetic principles and the Monte Carlo method, tuner stub heights were optimized to minimize power reflection, as quantified by the scattering parameter (S11).\n\nSeventeen processing conditions were simulated and validated against experimental data, showing prediction errors of 1.6\u202f\u00b1\u202f1.3\u00b0C for orange juice and between 1.8 and 5.5\u00b0C for mango puree and juice. Confined fluidized beds, originally conceptualized in the 1960s for other uses, are here investigated for their feasibility and effectiveness in increasing mass transfer when packed in gas other than air.\n\nExperiments involved four types of spherical packing solids, 6.35 to 25.4 mm in diameter, at two densities. Low-density packing materials demonstrated enhanced flotsam segregation, which, with increased fluidization velocities, promoted better mixing between packing and fluidizing solids within the confined bed packed in gas other than air. Additionally, maximum vertical crossflow of solids was significantly higher with fluidizable low-density packing compared to stationary high-density packing arrangements.\n\nIn conclusion, deploying confined fluidized beds with carefully selected packing solids in gas other than air shows significant promise to overcome mass transfer limitations in chemical looping combustion and related processes. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03315271": "This work addresses the challenge of simulating material cyclic plasticity behavior in components subjected to low-cycle fatigue loading, where modeling must continue until complete stabilization occurs at about half the number of cycles to failure. When plastic strain per cycle is small, simulating the full number of cycles becomes computationally expensive and time-consuming. Therefore, acceleration techniques for shortening the simulation time are important, though their accuracy requires verification.\n\nThe study compares different modeling approaches involving plasticity: nonlinear kinematic hardening with both \u201cinitial\u201d and \u201cstabilized\u201d parameters, and a combined nonlinear kinematic and isotropic model where the speed of stabilization is fictitiously increased to shorten the simulation time. Two benchmarks from literature, representing materials with opposite cyclic behaviors (hardening and softening of plastic strain), are analyzed using a plane finite element model, which allows simulation up to full stabilization.\n\nResults indicate that relying solely on a nonlinear kinematic plasticity model calibrated on either the initial or stabilized material state from the first cycle can produce significant inaccuracies. Conversely, the acceleration technique based on an artificially increased speed of plastic stabilization effectively shortens the simulation duration while maintaining accuracy. This method offers a reliable means to reduce the computational burden associated with cyclic plasticity simulations involving low-cycle fatigue.\n\nFinally, the work proposes guidelines for calibrating the fictitious acceleration of plastic stabilization speed, tailored to the material\u2019s cyclic hardening or softening plastic behavior. Overall, this study underscores the importance of carefully incorporating plasticity modeling and acceleration methods to shorten simulation times without compromising the accuracy of predicting cyclic plasticity and stabilization in materials under fatigue loading.",

This research was conducted in the absence of scuba diving tourism and fishing activities to observe natural behaviors. Among the swimming behaviors recorded, hovering, milling, and active swimming were noted, with milling occurring significantly more often. The rates of movement were lowest during milling and highest during active swimming. Grey sharks held their pectoral fins at angles between 20\u00b0 and 24\u00b0 below horizontal, aligning with fin positions documented in other shark swimming studies. During hovering, grey sharks exhibited significantly lower caudal fin positions, likely to minimize forward propulsion. Tail-beat frequency in grey sharks decreased notably as total length increased, probably due to the greater propulsion provided by larger caudal fins in bigger individuals. The observed low activity levels suggested that grey sharks reduce energy expenditure when aggregated, a behavior linked to migration and reproduction. Variations in pectoral fin positions among different sites were likely connected to different navigational demands faced by grey sharks. Non-swimming behaviors were rare; grooming behaviors included chafing, gill puff, head snapping, and palatoquadrate protrusion. A single gill puff sequence and almost all rapid withdrawal events were categorized as \u2018flight\u2019-response agonistic behaviors, while other rapid withdrawals and \u201cstand back\u201d movements were to avoid collisions and classified as swimming behaviors. Importantly, no \u2018fight\u2019-response agonistic behaviors were observed, reinforcing the characterization of grey sharks as docile. This partial ethogram of grey sharks not only advances ecological understanding but also aids in assessing and managing diving tourism impacts and supports the recovery and long-term conservation of this critically endangered species.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/HANCESTRO_0480": "The text discusses the behavior of tense/aspect/modal (TAM) markers in verb-initial Polynesian languages, focusing specifically on Tokelauan. It is traditionally understood, based on studies of languages such as Tongan and Samoan, that TAM markers originate in the T\u02da position and subsequently move to the C\u02da position through T-to-C movement. This movement results in a complementary distribution between TAM markers and complementisers, meaning they generally do not co-occur (Custis 2004; Otsuka 2005; Collins 2017). However, new data from Tokelauan challenge this assumption by showing that TAM particles and complementisers can appear together in the same clause. This discovery suggests that the T-to-C movement in Tokelauan\u2014and potentially other Polynesian languages\u2014is more complex than previously thought. To account for this, the text proposes an expanded left periphery in Tokelauan grammar, which includes two distinct complementiser positions. The TAM markers in Tokelauan are argued to raise to the lower of these complementiser sites, allowing for the observed co-occurrence of TAM particles and complementisers. Overall, the study of Tokelauan provides novel insights that complicate previous analyses of TAM and complementiser interaction in verb-initial Polynesian languages, highlighting the need for a more nuanced syntactic framework.",

Soft wheat kernels contain a high concentration of friabilin, distinguishing them from hard wheat kernels that have lower friabilin levels. This difference in friabilin concentration directly impacts the texture of the wheat kernel, with soft wheat kernels exhibiting a softer texture compared to their hard counterparts. The protein content in wheat, including soft wheat kernels, generally shows a positive correlation with kernel texture. Under Mid-European conditions, hard wheat typically contains about 12.0\u201313.0% crude protein and demonstrates a higher gluten content than soft wheat kernels. The texture of the kernel significantly influences milling properties, as hard-textured wheat grains require more grinding energy. In contrast, soft wheat kernels, due to their softer texture and higher friabilin concentration, need less power consumption during milling. This makes the soft wheat kernel advantageous in processes where lower grinding energy is preferred, affecting both the efficiency and outcome of milling operations. Overall, the soft wheat kernel's unique protein composition and texture characteristics play an essential role in determining its milling behavior and its distinction from hard wheat kernels.",

This process lowers internal muscle temperature rapidly and accelerates chilling, which benefits meat quality and safety. All operations follow stringent Sanitation Standard Operation Procedures (SSOP) and Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) programs, ensuring no reported food safety issues linked to RCT.\n\nThis technology is widely adapted across various meat types, including beef, bison meat food products, pork, and lamb, to enhance product safety, optimize meat quality, and improve economic performance. Specifically, in bison meat food products, RCT contributes to effective blood removal and favorable pH decline, which are critical for preserving the quality and integrity of the meat. By accelerating carcass chilling in bison and other species, RCT reduces bacterial growth and improves shelf life without chemical residues.\n\nOverall, this review highlights how RCT functions technically on bison meat food products alongside other major livestock types, emphasizing its role in improving meat processing outcomes without compromising safety or quality. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03510104": "This review by Ahmed Abdulrahman Alsunni from Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University examines the current state of research on artificial sweeteners (ASs) and their impact on glucose homeostasis, obesity, and type 2 diabetes (T2D). ASs are widely used for their ability to provide sweetness with minimal to no calories, making them popular choices for reducing energy intake and combating obesity. Despite their popularity, concerns persist about their safety and potential metabolic effects, particularly regarding interference with glucose regulation.\n\nThe review highlights that numerous studies have attempted to establish a connection between AS consumption and metabolic diseases such as obesity and T2D. However, these studies often suffer from significant methodological flaws, inconsistent designs, and lack of follow-up research, resulting in haphazard claims that are not reliably substantiated. Consequently, there remains no artificial sweeteners claim that conclusively links AS intake with adverse effects on glucose metabolism, obesity, or T2D.\n\nIt is emphasized that while it cannot be definitively claimed that ASs are metabolically inert, the existing body of evidence is insufficient to support any firm conclusions about their harmful effects. The current state of knowledge does not allow for a definitive no artificial sweeteners claim regarding metabolic safety concerns. To resolve this ambiguity, the review calls for well-designed cohort and case\u2013control studies with adequate sample sizes and rigorous methodologies to either establish a causal relationship or confidently exclude safety issues related to AS consumption.\n\nIn summary, the review underscores the absence of a clear no artificial sweeteners claim linking AS use to detrimental metabolic outcomes, highlighting the need for more robust and comprehensive research to clarify this important public health question.\n\nKeywords: artificial sweeteners, glucose, diabetes, obesity, no artificial sweeteners claim.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_02021503": "The common hippopotamus, Hippopotamus amphibius, plays a significant ecological role by transporting millions of tons of organic matter annually from terrestrial feeding grounds to aquatic habitats. This study investigated whether carbon stable isotopes (\u03b413C) can serve as reliable tracers to determine if aquatic consumers utilize hippopotamus material, specifically H. amphibius-vectored allochthonous organic matter. Two main approaches were used: (1) controlled lab feeding trials where omnivorous river fish were fed a diet consisting solely of H. amphibius dung, and (2) field sampling of fish and aquatic insects in river pools with and without the presence of H. amphibius. Results from the lab trials showed that fish consuming only H. amphibius dung had significantly more positive \u03b413C values compared to those not fed dung, indicating incorporation of hippopotamus material into their tissues. Field data supported these findings; fish and aquatic insects collected from a pool inhabited by H. amphibius for decades exhibited more positive \u03b413C values at the end of the dry season relative to organisms sampled from an upstream reference pool devoid of hippopotamus material. However, during the wet season characterized by high flow, no significant \u03b413C differences were observed between the pools, implying that increased water flow reduced the retention and utilization of H. amphibius subsidies. Collectively, these findings provide preliminary evidence that \u03b413C signatures could potentially be used to trace and quantify the importance of H. amphibius organic matter in aquatic food webs under specific environmental conditions. This highlights the ecological significance of hippopotamus material as a subsidy that influences aquatic consumer diets and suggests stable isotope analysis as a method to assess the incorporation of hippopotamus-derived organic matter in riverine ecosystems.",

Depending on its botanical source, caffeine is known by various names such as guaranine (from guarana seeds), matein (from yerba mate), and theine (from tea leaves). Coffee and tea are two of the most common caffeine-containing beverages worldwide, frequently consumed to alleviate mental and physical fatigue.\n\nUpon oral intake, caffeine is rapidly and almost completely absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, especially the small intestine. It is then distributed throughout the body, penetrating all tissues and entering the water space of cells. The liver metabolizes nearly all ingested caffeine, with only about 2% excreted unchanged via the kidneys. Factors influencing caffeine metabolism include genetics, age, gender, pregnancy, diet, lifestyle, smoking, environmental influences, medications, and various diseases.\n\nCaffeine is not only a key component of coffee and tea but is also added to carbonated drinks like Pepsi and Coca-Cola, energy drinks, and numerous medications. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved caffeine for medical use in treating apnea and preventing bronchopulmonary dysplasia in premature infants. While caffeine consumption from coffee and tea plants has various positive and negative effects on the body, individual responses to caffeine can vary widely.\n\nIn summary, caffeine derived from coffee and tea plants is one of the most commonly consumed psychoactive substances globally, valued for its stimulating properties and widespread presence in daily beverages and medications. Its pharmacokinetics, metabolism, and effects are influenced by multiple internal and external factors, underscoring the individual variability in caffeine consumption and response.",

This study developed a novel approach to predict the storage time of frozen Antarctic krill to assess its quality quickly. Over a 12-month storage period, traditional chemical quality indicators of krill were monitored, confirming a clear correlation between quality deterioration and storage time. To enhance prediction accuracy, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) data from frozen Antarctic krill samples were analyzed using four different regression machine learning algorithms. This correspondence confirms the model\u2019s reliability and its ability to effectively capture the quality dynamics of frozen krill over time. The findings validate that combining NIR spectroscopy with the LightGBM algorithm offers a rapid, non-destructive, and precise technique for evaluating the quality and storage duration of frozen Antarctic krill. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03304175": "Stretch-shortening cycles (SSCs) describe a muscle action where an active muscle stretch (eccentric contraction) is immediately followed by active muscle shortening (concentric contraction). This combination is crucial for daily muscle activities and plays a vital role in natural locomotion such as walking, running, and jumping across both humans and animals. SSCs are particularly important in movements requiring high speed or energy efficiency, with the concentric phase showing more than a 50% increase in muscular force and work compared to concentric actions without prior stretch\u2014known as the SSC-effect.\n\nThe enhanced muscle performance during SSCs is attributed to several mechanisms including pre-activation of muscles, stretch-reflex responses, and elastic recoil from serial elastic components. A significant contribution is also thought to come from sarcomeric structures within muscles. To investigate this, the study examined force output and work produced by single skinned fibers of rat soleus muscles during shortening, lengthening, and stretch-shortening cycles under physiological conditions. SSC magnitudes involved 18% stretch of optimum muscle length and shortening was performed at 85% of maximum velocity.\n\nUsing Blebbistatin to differentiate the contributions of cross-bridge (XB) and non-cross-bridge (non-XB) structures, three key findings emerged: (i) partial detachment of XBs during the eccentric phase of the SSC, (ii) significantly increased force and mechanical work during the concentric phase of SSCs compared to shortening contractions, both with and without XB inhibition, and (iii) absence of residual force depression after SSCs.\n\nThe results suggest a titin-actin interaction that depends on XB binding and active cross-bridge force production. Enhanced forces generated during the active lengthening phase of stretch-shortening cycles persist into the subsequent shortening phase, contributing to increased mechanical work. This supports the hypothesis that sarcomeric mechanisms related to residual force enhancement contribute to the SSC-effect. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03304361": "Mango nectar is a commercially popular and preferred fruit product traditionally processed using thermal methods. However, thermal processing, typically involving heating at 96 \u00baC for extended durations (300 to 600 seconds), negatively impacts mango nectar by altering its flavor due to high temperature exposure. This process not only reduces the sensory and nutritive qualities of mango nectar but also leads to the formation of unwanted byproducts such as 5-hydroxy methyl furfural (HMF), a compound associated with non-enzymatic browning. The presence of HMF increases with both thermal treatment and storage time, further diminishing the quality of mango nectar.\n\nIn response to the drawbacks of thermal processing, there is growing interest in alternative non-thermal technologies like pulsed electric field (PEF) treatment. The present study explored the use of PEF to process mango nectar in order to minimize volatile compound loss and reduce HMF formation. The experimental conditions included thermal processing (96 \u00baC for 300 and 600 seconds), PEF treatment (24 microseconds pulse duration, 120 Hz frequency, and 38 kV/cm field strength), and a combination of PEF followed by a shorter thermal treatment (PEF + thermal at 96 \u00baC for 90 seconds).\n\nVolatile composition analysis of mango nectar using GC-MS revealed that samples subjected to thermal and combination processing exhibited a significant reduction in volatile compounds (p < 0.05), which are crucial for the flavor profile of mango nectar. In contrast, mango nectar treated with PEF alone retained most of its volatile compounds, indicating a better preservation of its fresh-like aroma and flavor. HPLC measurements of HMF showed that the lowest levels were found in the PEF-treated mango nectar, with values not significantly different (p > 0.05) from those in unprocessed samples, highlighting the advantage of PEF in maintaining the quality of mango nectar.\n\nOverall, the study demonstrates that PEF treatment of mango nectar effectively preserves its sensory and nutritive attributes by reducing the loss of volatiles and limiting HMF formation, offering a promising alternative to conventional thermal processing for producing fresh-like mango nectar.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03413226": "The EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings (FAF) conducted a scientific re-evaluation of the safety of propane-1,2-diol esters of fatty acids (E 477) as a food additive. The acceptable daily intake (ADI) of 25 mg/kg body weight (bw) per day, expressed as propane-1,2-diol, was originally endorsed by the Scientific Committee on Food (SCF) in 1978 and established by the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) in 1974. Short-term toxicity studies in rats and dogs at high doses showed no adverse effects. The Panel concluded that propane-1,2-diol esters of fatty acids (E 477) do not pose genotoxicity concerns. However, no chronic toxicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive, or developmental toxicity studies specifically on propane-1,2-diol esters of fatty acids were available.\n\nThe Panel reasoned that any potential adverse effects of propane-1,2-diol esters of fatty acids would be attributable to propane-1,2-diol itself, for which an ADI of 25 mg/kg bw per day has been established. Based on the overall metabolism and toxicity data, the Panel confirmed the previously established ADI for propane-1,2-diol esters of fatty acids (E 477) of 25 mg/kg bw per day expressed as propane-1,2-diol. This corresponds to an ADI of 80 mg/kg bw per day for E 477, considering the maximum concentration of free and bound propane-1,2-diol at 31% according to EU specifications.\n\nThe Panel concluded there is no safety concern for propane-1,2-diol esters of fatty acids (E 477) at reported use levels, as exposure estimates from refined non-brand loyal scenarios did not exceed the ADI in any population group. Looking forward, the Panel intends to explore establishing a group ADI for food additives resulting in exposure to propane-1,2-diol, such as E 477, E 1520, and E 405, and considers performing a combined exposure assessment to propane-1,2-diol from these additives. Additionally, the Panel recommended modifications to the EU specifications for propane-1,2-diol esters of fatty acids (E 477).",

This maximization is subject to constraints ensuring that the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) requirements of the CUs are met, all while adhering to the power limits of the HAPS platform.\n\nCompared with traditional terrestrial and UAV-based ISAC systems, HAPS-ISAC offers sustained and reliable coverage over large geographical areas. This leads to significantly improved system metrics, including SINR improvement, efficient resource allocation, enhanced sensing accuracy, and increased fairness among users. The integration of MISO configurations within the MIMO framework is a critical enabler of these advancements, allowing for effective communication beamforming and sensing simultaneously.\n\nSimulation results validate the superiority of HAPS-ISAC over existing technologies, positioning it as a key enabler for 6G network deployment. Furthermore, the system's capabilities advance intelligent infrastructure development such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and smart cities, supporting the future landscape of connected and autonomous technologies.\n\nIn summary, the proposed HAPS-ISAC system utilizes MISO and MIMO architectures to optimize dual communication and sensing performance in a high-altitude platform, providing robust 6G network support with broad-area coverage, improved SINR, and sensing precision.",

Within the structure, there are two distinct phosphorus atom sites, each tetrahedrally coordinated by four oxygen atoms. These phosphate tetrahedra share a common oxygen atom, creating the diphosphate units characteristic of disodium diphosphate. The nickel ions exhibit a square pyramidal coordination environment with four oxygen atoms sourced from two diphosphate groups occupying the equatorial positions, while a water oxygen atom sits at the pyramid\u2019s apex. The disodium diphosphate (P2O7)(H2O) units serve as bridges linking the nickel atoms, forming chains composed of alternating pyramidal and tetrahedral units. The crystal symmetry, defined by the d-glide and twofold-axis in space group Fdd2, directs the propagation of these chains along the [101] and [10overline{1}] directions, with adjacent chains arranged orthogonally. Additionally, the calcium and sodium cations\u2014components of the compound\u2019s disodium diphosphate framework\u2014are each coordinated octahedrally by four oxygen atoms and two water molecules. This coordination helps stabilize the nickel chains. The overall Ni-chain structure is further reinforced through a hydrogen-bonding network involving O\u2013H\u00b7\u00b7\u00b7O interactions, integral to the stability of the disodium diphosphate-containing lattice. Thus, the compound\u2019s architecture is defined by the interplay of disodium diphosphate units, metal cations, and coordinated water molecules, culminating in a stable, three-dimensional framework.",

Water contact angle measurements demonstrated that both tangerine peel flour and TA altered surface wettability, generally decreasing the water contact angle and indicating increased hydrophilicity. Importantly, biodegradability tests showed that all composites containing tangerine peel flour and/or TA achieved complete disintegration under controlled compost soil conditions within 5 weeks, whereas neat PLA required 6 weeks for full disintegration. To address this, the research explores the use of computer vision systems to non-invasively and efficiently assess key parameters such as size, weight, volume, and grade of poultry meat. Specifically, the study developed mathematical prediction models for turkey meat yield utilizing a real-time 2D imaging system applied to 4,000 turkey carcasses. This represents an initial advancement in applying imaging technology for practical turkey carcass portion prediction. Enhancing the ability to predict carcass yields beyond relying on live turkey weight could help the turkey industry collect phenotypic data more cost-effectively and accurately. Literature searches across six electronic databases up to June 2023 identified 75 articles, with 10 RCTs meeting inclusion criteria for assessing the impact of daily olive oil polyphenol consumption on serum lipids in adults.\n\nThe studies, mostly European and healthy populations, used polyphenol doses categorized into tertiles for HDL-C, LDL-C, and total cholesterol (TC) outcomes. This finding supports a cautiously positive reduced cholesterol claim specifically for LDL-C at higher polyphenol doses.\n\nAdditionally, a statistically significant increase in HDL cholesterol (HDL-C) was noted across all polyphenol intake levels \u2014 low, medium, and high \u2014 with weighted mean differences (WMD) ranging from 0.66 to 1.36 mg/dL, further indicating olive oil polyphenols contribute beneficially to lipid metabolism. This HDL-C enhancement strengthens the evidence base supporting health claims related to lipid profile improvement.\n\nOverall, the data suggest olive oil polyphenols modestly contribute to maintaining lipid metabolism, primarily through modest LDL-C reduction at high intakes and consistent HDL-C elevation. The findings advocate for food labeling regulations to include declarations of olive oil polyphenol content, enabling consumers to make informed choices based on quality and potential health benefits. Illegal or improper disposal of deer carcasses at sites such as the one studied can lead to significant contamination of soil with infectious prions, thereby facilitating ongoing transmission of CWD among wild and captive cervid populations. The persistence of prions from deer carcasses in the environment indicates the importance of implementing proper carcass management to mitigate the risk of sustained CWD spread. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03510266": "Food allergies are immunologically mediated hypersensitivity reactions, also known as food hypersensitivity, caused by the immune system responding to specific food proteins. The eight most common food allergens include proteins from milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, soya, wheat, fish, and shellfish, although other foods like certain fruits, vegetables, and seeds can also act as allergens. These allergens pose a significant food safety concern, prompting regulatory requirements in the European Union mandating that allergenic ingredients be clearly labeled to protect allergic consumers.\n\nApproximately 8% of children and 4% of adults suffer from food allergies, with many food allergies developing during infancy or early childhood. Infants as food consumers are particularly vulnerable, with allergies often affecting the gastrointestinal tract, including the stomach and intestines. Some allergies may persist into adulthood, such as coeliac disease, an abnormal immune reaction to gluten proteins found in wheat and barley.\n\nAlmost all food allergens are proteins, and sensitive analytical techniques have been developed to detect minute traces of these allergens in food. These methods include electrophoretic and immunological techniques, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. Detecting allergenicity is crucial not only for the safety of infants as consumers\u2014who are frequently affected by early-onset food allergies\u2014but also for protecting allergic individuals of all ages.\n\nThis review aims to detail the allergenic components of the most common food allergens and discusses their significance for the food industry and consumer safety, with particular attention to the sensitive detection methods required. The emphasis on infants as food consumers highlights the critical importance of early identification and management of food allergies to prevent adverse reactions during this vulnerable stage of development.",

These cave crickets are primarily found in humid microhabitats such as caves and wet forests. Despite their widespread presence, the true diversity of cave crickets remains poorly understood. In Australia, 27 species of these crickets have been described from nine genera within the subfamily Macropathinae, with the highest diversity located in Tasmania, a mesic island state. Among these, the genus Micropathus Richards, 1964, is the most widespread cricket genus on the island and includes five species mainly confined to subterranean habitats.\n\nMicropathus cave crickets depend on pockets of relictual wet forest, rendering them vulnerable to threats like climate change and land use modifications. One species of Micropathus cave cricket is listed as Critically Endangered because of these risks. A recent molecular phylogeny focused on Macropathinae cave crickets identified two additional, putatively undescribed Micropathus cricket species. These newly recognized species cannot be properly conserved without formal scientific descriptions. Combining morphological data with phylogenetic analysis, researchers formally describe two new Micropathus cave cricket species: Micropathus ditto Beasley-Hall sp. nov., which was previously mistaken for a subpopulation of Micropathus tasmaniensis, and Micropathus zubat Beasley-Hall sp. nov., currently known only from the remote Forest Hills karst system.\n\nThis work also provides a taxonomic key to Micropathus cave crickets and redescribes existing species to better capture intraspecific morphological variation within the genus. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03543276": "what do children choosing sweets in a shop and their adults selecting fruits in a grocery have in common? both use the appearance and decide to buy the most colorful items. this very daily example shows that the colors of foods have a strong influence on our perception of acceptability and palatability (blendford, 1995; hendry and houghton, 1996; newsome, 1990). \"plant pigment\" is a generic expression used to designate a large number of colored molecules synthesized by photosynthetic organisms. on the basis of their chemical structure, they can be classified into four families: tetrapyrroles (e.g., chlorophyll), carotenoids (e.g., \u03b2-carotene), polyphenolic compounds (e.g., anthocyanins), and alkaloids (e.g., betalains). an example of the chemical structure of a member of each family of compounds is presented in figure 1. the number of molecules belonging to each family is quite large, so several volumes would be necessary to describe their particular properties. the description of the physicochemical properties of pigments has been the topic of comprehensive reviews and books (britton, 1988; britton et al., 1995; gross, 1991; schoefs, 2002). plant pigments have positive roles in human health (franceschi et al., 1994; gerster, 1993; groten et al., 2000; kumpulainen and salonen, 1996; mayne et al., 1994; shim et al., 2003). although animal tissues contain plant pigments, these tissues are not able to synthesize them. therefore, the pigments must be obtained from food (baker, 1992; castenmiller et al., 1999; depee et al., 1998). once assimilated, pigments enter the biochemical pathways along which they may be eventually modified (parkinson and brown, 1981). for instance, \u03b2-carotene is split into two parts, one of these serving as a precursor of vitamin a (goswani and barua, 2003), an important molecule for vision, skin protection, and cell growth. several studies have established the minimum daily intake of these valuable pigment molecules. because consumption of fresh foods has decreased and that of processed foods has increased, food colors have become an important aspect of the pigment food formulation process. unfortunately, during food processing, the natural pigment content may be altered or destroyed. a very demonstrative example is the color change that occurs during the processing of mangoes or pineapple flesh. in the fresh fruit, the main carotenoid is the diepoxy-carotenoid violaxanthin (yellow), which during processing is transformed to the faint-yellow auroxanthin, a furanoid carotenoid (mercadante and rodriguez-amaya, 1998) (see figure 4). to restore the natural level in pigments in the processed products, extracted pigments are incorporated into the final food products (britton, 1995; burton and ingold, 1984; garcia-viguera et al., 2000; palozza and krinsky, 1991). similarly the preparation of fortified products requires the addition of pigments to the products (smith, 1991). regardless of the type of final products, the pigments are incorporated either as they naturally occur or as a chemically modified form (e.g., chlorophyllin or glycosylation of crocetin) (dufresne et al., 1999). as a consequence of these additional needs, the demand in natural colorants has increased compared to synthetic dyes (joppen, 2003; pszczola, 1988). however, this increase cannot always be satisfied due to the limited supply of raw materials because the production of pigments using conventional plant cultivation methods is influenced by climatic conditions, plant cultivars, and varieties (rodriguez-amaya, 2000). consequently part of plant pigment research is oriented to finding new sources of pigments. this quest is not only directed toward finding natural alternatives to synthetic dyes but also with the aim to discover new taxons and new procedures to produce pigments, for instance, from cell cultures (table i). pigment production by cell or microalgal cultures is especially interesting because these methods can be established independently of the climatic influences. in addition, yields can be predicted (rodriguez-amaya, 2000) and eventually improved by applications of elicitors or through genetic engineering (ye et al., 2000). for all the reasons cited previously, pigment analysis constitutes a real analytical challenge. to take this challenge, one must have a diversified number of analytical procedures able to rapidly and precisely quantify the different pigment levels in samples. addressing these issues is never straightforward. with some samples, like bottled waters, analysis is very simple. other samples are highly complex mixtures, requiring careful processing and storage conditions to ensure an unchanged level of pigments and color. this is especially important in the case of fortified foods, which create nutritional expectations from both the health authorities and the consumers. the development of powerful analytical methods is also of prime importance in the control of quality. obviously, this requires a precise knowledge of the pigment composition of original products (mercadante et al., 1998; minguez-mosquera et al., 1995a). in this contribution, the molecular structures, the general physicochemical properties of plant pigments, and the mechanisms involved in pigment degradation are first described. then follows a review on invasive and noninvasive methods used for pigment analysis, including the mechanisms involved in pigment degradation. finally, several examples of analytical procedures are presented. \u00a9 2005 elsevier inc. all rights reserved.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03500037": "This study explores the thermal and mechanical behavior of friction stir spot welding (FSSW) for joining dissimilar thermoplastics, specifically focusing on the polyvinyl chloride (PVC) surface and polyethylene (PE). Due to the significant differences in their polarity, crystallinity, melting temperatures, and surface energies, achieving strong bonding between the polyvinyl chloride surface and polyethylene is challenging. The experimental approach involved varying the FSSW process parameters\u2014rotational speed and dwell time\u2014and evaluating the effects through tensile shear testing and infrared thermal analysis.\n\nKey findings indicate that the rotational speed notably influences the peak interfacial temperature at the polyvinyl chloride surface, reaching up to 137\u00b0C. This temperature surpasses the crystalline melting range of both PVC (75\u2013105\u00b0C) and PE (130\u2013135\u00b0C), enabling localized melting at the polyvinyl chloride surface. Such melting promotes effective molecular interdiffusion at the weld interface, facilitating robust bonding between the polyvinyl chloride surface and polyethylene without the need for external adhesives or surface treatments.\n\nUsing Taguchi-based design of experiments (DOE) analysis, the study identified optimal welding conditions\u20141700 RPM rotational speed and a 2-minute dwell time\u2014that yielded the highest joint strength and temperature at the polyvinyl chloride surface interface. Tensile shear strength results further confirmed that appropriate heat input and tool interaction are critical for attaining durable bonds involving the polyvinyl chloride surface.\n\nOverall, this research provides valuable insights into optimizing FSSW parameters for joining polyvinyl chloride surfaces with polyethylene, offering an environmentally friendly, scalable alternative to traditional adhesive methods. The findings have potential applications across packaging, automotive, and biomedical industries where strong, reliable bonding of polyvinyl chloride surfaces to dissimilar thermoplastics is essential.",

The study emphasizes an urgent need for structured mental health programs tailored to individuals working in animal rescue shelters. Implementing support groups, therapeutic options, and workplace well-being initiatives is essential to combat compassion fatigue and burnout, subsequently improving employee retention, job satisfaction, and the quality of animal care within these settings. However, fuzzy control has been found to produce unstable responses and irregular stove flames. To address these issues, the Low Temperature Long Time (LTLT) pasteurization method is employed and automatically controlled using a PID control system. The LTLT pasteurization technique is key in maintaining milk\u2019s nutritional quality by keeping the temperature steady at a setpoint of 62\u00b0C.\n\nThe automation of the LTLT pasteurization process involves servo actuators and electric lighters regulated via flame sensors. These flame sensors monitor the flame's presence to ensure it remains lit throughout the pasteurization cycle. Positioned within 10 cm of the flame source, the sensor generates an analog output with a maximum reading of 4000 when the flame is active, and a higher value of 4095 when the flame goes out. Testing these PID values resulted in a rise time of 0.39 minutes, a settling time range between 60.88 and 62.38 minutes, and a minimal overshoot of 0.61%. Of these, 2,365 were waterbirds, with ducks making up 91.8% (2,173) and green-winged teals comprising 93.5% of the ducks. The rapid collection and removal of avian animal material (dead and sick birds) combined with flooding of the wetland appeared to end the 2019 botulism emergency.\n\nIn May and July 2020, two water inputs were recorded; only one pooled sample from 16 bird carcasses detected clostridia type C by real-time PCR. Despite initial control measures, new avian botulism cases attributed to clostridia type C and C/D were confirmed by molecular and animal-model tests. In high PA diets, CS+AC produced the highest milk fat and FCM yields, and AC increased milk fat yield over CON and CS. The basal diet with high PA alone achieved milk fat yields comparable to AC and CS+AC treatments in low PA diets, highlighting PA\u2019s crucial role in stimulating milk triglyceride synthesis. Alaska) and its agravitropic mutant, ageotropum. Traditionally, apical hook formation is thought to be influenced by gravity, but this belief mainly stems from studies on the hypocotyl hook, with limited research on the epicotyl hook\u2019s developmental dynamics. Time-course experiments under normal 1-g conditions and on a 3-D clinostat demonstrated that in Alaska pea, the epicotyl hook forms from the arc-shaped plumule present within the ungerminated seed. The hook formation proceeds through two intrinsic stages\u2014development and partial opening\u2014independent of gravity. Around the time the epicotyl emerges from the seed coat, the hook is fully established in both Alaska pea and the ageotropum mutant. In Alaska pea, gravity sustains or enhances the established hook, delaying its opening compared to conditions on the clinostat; this delay may have led to the misconception that gravity induces hook formation. Both Alaska pea and ageotropum maintain the orientation of the original plumular arc during hook development and opening, with the hook consistently positioned on the same side of the epicotyl axis as the cotyledons, irrespective of gravitational conditions. Furthermore, application of auxin polar transport inhibitors\u2014hydroxyfluorenecarboxylic acid, naphthylphthalamic acid, and triiodobenzoic acid\u2014equally suppressed hook curvature in Alaska pea and ageotropum, indicating that auxin polar transport, likely asymmetrically distributed across the plumular axis due to intrinsic plumule properties, governs hook development independently of gravity. Notably, anomalous chemical values were confined to areas immediately surrounding the seal carcasses. The findings suggest that concentrated seal carcasses, especially in wetter microhabitats within an otherwise semi-desert climate, serve as crucial nutrient oases. These seal carcasses induce a combination of physical and chemical effects throughout their decomposition stages, enhancing conditions favorable for plant establishment and succession. For comparison, the dielectric constant of the base sunflower oil was measured while being stored in a glass container at room temperature without light exposure.\n\nResults indicated that the dielectric constant of the vegetable-based heating liquid in container increases linearly during the oxidation process. This increase in permittivity corresponds with a rise in the number of polar molecules, caused by the formation of secondary oxidation products. Temperature-induced chemical changes in the heating liquid in container lead to the creation of primary oxidation products, such as hydroperoxides. Notably, oxidation products from the vegetable-based heating liquid in container do not precipitate; instead, the oil thickens and polymerizes.\n\nThe developed diagnostic method for insulating liquids is based on determining a coefficient proportional to the growth rate of polar molecules in the heating liquid in container. Findings reveal that monitoring only the tangent of dielectric losses does not reliably indicate the state of vegetable-based oil or its oxidative processes. Conversely, the steady increase in the dielectric constant during thermal oxidation of the heating liquid in container clearly reflects the chemical changes related to polymerization.\n\nIn summary, cyclic heating liquid in container simulating transformer tank conditions effectively models the thermal oxidation of vegetable-based oil, highlighting the dielectric constant as a key parameter for monitoring oil condition and oxidation behavior.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03510131": "This study examines the regulation of label claims, particularly focusing on the term \"less\" label claim, within Sri Lanka\u2019s Food (Labelling and Advertising) Regulations, 2005, under the Food Act of 1980. Label claims are a major marketing strategy in the food industry; however, inaccurate or misleading claims, including those related to \"less\" claims, can negatively impact consumer health, necessitating strict regulatory oversight.\n\nThe analysis identifies significant shortcomings in the current Sri Lankan regulations concerning food claims. Notably, the regulations are described as less strong and less precisely structured compared to international standards such as Codex Alimentarius and regulations in developed countries like Australia. The scope and definition of \"claim\" are vague in the Sri Lankan legal context, with limited types of claims recognized and often misclassified. Importantly, certain claim types, including various \"less\" claims that indicate reduced amounts of certain ingredients (e.g., less fat, less sugar), are not clearly defined or adequately covered by the existing framework.\n\nDue to these deficiencies, the study highlights that Sri Lanka\u2019s current legislative approach offers less comprehensive protection for consumers against misleading or inaccurate \"less\" label claims. In comparison, international regulations present broader, more detailed, and stronger guidelines that better safeguard public health.\n\nTo address these issues, the study recommends amending the Food (Labelling and Advertising) Regulations to include broader, clearer, and stronger provisions for all types of claims, especially \u201cless\u201d label claims. Strengthening the regulations will help align Sri Lanka with global best practices, reduce ambiguities, and ensure that claims such as \"less fat\" or \"less sugar\" are accurately and consistently regulated. Ultimately, such improvements are necessary to enhance consumer protection and promote public health by limiting the potential for misleading use of \"less\" label claims in food marketing.",
