"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03460270": "Membrane distillation (MD) is a promising food distillation process used in various applications, including drinking water treatment, seawater desalination, ultra-pure water production, chemical concentration, removal or recovery of volatile solutes, concentration of fruit juice or liquid food, and wastewater treatment. Nonetheless, studies addressing momentum transfer, heat, and mass transfer within membrane pores\u2014a critical component of the food distillation process\u2014are limited. Comprehensive research combining these transfer mechanisms is essential for advancing the understanding of this food distillation process.\n\nMoreover, some physical phenomena significant to the food distillation process, such as surface diffusion on membrane surfaces, are often neglected in CFD simulations despite their importance for novel membrane development. Although CFD simulations are widely applied in modeling the food distillation process, challenges remain, warranting further investigation.\n\nFuture CFD modeling of the food distillation process is expected to incorporate more complex mechanisms, including permeable wall conditions, fouling dynamics, and multiple ionic component diffusion. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_00003313": "The fungal genus Alternar\u00eda is widely distributed in soil and decomposing organic matter, comprising saprophytic, endophytic, and pathogenic species. Several Alternar\u00eda species are plant pathogens that invade crops both before and after harvest, causing significant yield reductions and economic losses. These fungi produce over 70 secondary metabolites known as phytotoxins, many of which are toxic not only to plants but also to humans and animals, thus considered mycotoxins. Exposure to Alternar\u00eda toxins has been associated with adverse health effects, including genotoxicity, mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, and cytotoxicity. \n\nAlternar\u00eda mycotoxins have been isolated from a variety of fruits such as apple, pear, melon, apricot, grapes, raisins, strawberry, olive, citrus fruits, dried figs, and notably in vegetables including raw pear tomato, pepper, and carrot, as well as tubers like potato. According to this model, HMF is generated exclusively through the dehydration of fructose, which is derived from sucrose. Side products form simultaneously from glucose, fructose, and HMF, indicating competing reaction pathways. Additionally, the model accounts for a pathway where hexoses convert to xylose via a reverse aldol reaction.\n\nThe study highlights the central role of fructose derived from sucrose in HMF synthesis. Since HMF production proceeds primarily through the dehydration of fructose, the availability and conversion dynamics of fructose from sucrose are critical. The research supports the notion that sucrose is an ideal feedstock for the large-scale production of HMF, given its greater abundance compared to fructose alone and its easier processing relative to sugars from lignocellulosic biomass. These by-products were prepared as either ground mass or dry powder and incorporated into six different forcemeat sample types, varying in proportions and combination, alongside a control sample without any additive. The findings suggest that incorporating chicken by-products into forcemeat can beneficially improve its physical and chemical characteristics, thus enhancing the overall quality of the forcemeat products. Furthermore, this practice offers potential cost-effectiveness and sustainability benefits by reducing poultry waste. Overall, the study demonstrates that strategic use of chicken feet and heads, particularly in powder form, can be a valuable approach to optimizing forcemeat formulations without compromising structural integrity.",

Later, at 8 months old, accidental ingestion of an extensively hydrolyzed casein/whey formula named MA-mi led to watery diarrhea, helping confirm the FPIES diagnosis. Interestingly, antigen-specific lymphocyte stimulation tests showed positive reactions to cow's milk antigens and MA-mi but negative reactions to another extensively hydrolyzed casein formula, New MA-1. This indicated that the causative allergens were derived solely from cow's milk proteins, with no symptoms triggered by New MA-1.\n\nWhile the infant's symptoms were related to cow's milk protein and not infant food based on soy protein, the discussion emphasizes caution regarding the use of specialized infant formulas like MA-mi in allergic infants. MA-mi\u2019s growing use among allergy-prone infants does not guarantee it as a suitable substitute for other hydrolyzed milk formulas in all cases. This highlights the complexity of managing FPIES and the need for careful selection of infant foods, including those based on soy protein or hydrolyzed milk components, tailored to each infant's specific allergenic profile.\n\nUltimately, the infant in this case grew and developed normally without further symptoms induced by solid foods or infant food based on soy protein during the course of the condition. The report underlines the necessity for precise diagnosis and cautious feeding practices in infants with FPIES, especially regarding the introduction of various formulas and allergenic infant foods based on soy protein or milk-derived proteins.",

This disruption breaks the stable sol system of sesame butter and peanut butter, enabling rapid stratification and quick release of the oil. The improved method involves mixing the sesame butter sample with acetone-water solution (1:1 volume ratio, sample to solvent mass/volume ratio 1:1), followed by addition of petroleum ether at three times the sample volume. These improvements result in greater accuracy and reliability in determining the acid value and peroxide value of sesame butter and peanut butter products. Precision and accuracy analyses confirm that this method is dependable for extracting oils from sesame butter and peanut butter for quality assessment.\n\nIn summary, the novel extraction procedure effectively addresses the inefficiencies of traditional oil extraction from sesame butter and peanut butter, offering a rapid, efficient, and accurate approach for oil extraction prior to acid value and peroxide value testing in these products.",

Additionally, blood samples were analyzed for stable isotopes, particularly \u03b415N, to infer dietary patterns.\n\nChinstrap penguins exhibited significant interannual variation, diving deeper, covering larger foraging areas, and showing enriched \u03b415N values in 2014/15 compared to 2017/18. In contrast, macaroni (enriched) penguins maintained consistent diving depths and \u03b415N values across both seasons, while consistently exploiting larger foraging areas than chinstraps. The study suggests that low krill abundance around Bouvet\u00f8ya in 2014/15 caused chinstrap penguins to shift their diet, increasing niche overlap with macaroni (enriched) penguins.\n\nThese findings highlight the role of macaroni (enriched) penguins in shaping niche dynamics under fluctuating environmental conditions and suggest that dietary shifts by chinstrap penguins may be associated with their declining breeding numbers on Bouvet\u00f8ya. The consistent foraging patterns of macaroni (enriched) penguins contrast with the plasticity observed in chinstraps, emphasizing the importance of multi-season data to fully characterize niche overlap and interspecific competition among these species. Understanding the ecological interplay involving macaroni (enriched) penguins provides valuable insight into how resource availability and spatial limitations influence predator coexistence on isolated islands.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03414748": "The lace plant (<i>Aponogeton madagascariensis</i>) serves as a valuable model for studying developmentally regulated programmed cell death (PCD) in plants. This process, crucial for the formation of perforations in the leaves, occurs between longitudinal and transverse veins within areas called areoles. In the <i>Aponogeton</i> plant, PCD initiates centrally in the areoles and progresses outward, creating a discernible gradient of cell death. To investigate this sequence, both long- and short-term live cell imaging alongside histochemical staining were employed.\n\nIn the <i>Aponogeton</i> plant, the earliest detectable change during PCD is the reduction of anthocyanin pigmentation, followed by alterations in chloroplasts and the bundling of actin microfilaments. At this stage, an increase in transvacuolar strands is noted, along with heightened numbers of vesicles, small mitochondrial aggregates, and the perinuclear accumulation of chloroplasts and mitochondria. These vesicles contained organelle materials, indicating both micro- and macro-autophagy are involved in the process. Mitochondrial aggregates and individual chloroplasts eventually exhibit Brownian motion within the vacuole. Subsequent key events in the <i>Aponogeton</i> plant include fragmentation of nuclear DNA, breakdown of actin microfilaments, and early changes in the cell wall.\n\nA major event is vacuole swelling that displaces the nucleus toward the plasma membrane (PM), culminating in tonoplast rupture which signals mega-autophagy. After this rupture, Brownian motion ceases, mitochondrial membrane potential is lost, and the nucleus shrinks before the plasma membrane collapses\u2014this final stage lasting roughly 20 minutes. The entire PCD process from chlorophyll reduction to plasma membrane collapse spans about 48 hours in the lace plant. Additionally, around six hours post-PM collapse, the cell wall begins to disappear, completing within 24 hours.\n\nOverall, the <i>Aponogeton</i> plant exhibits a consistent, well-defined sequence of cellular events during its developmental PCD, making it an excellent system for in vivo studies and comparative analyses with other plant developmental PCD instances.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_00003456": "The increasing global population has led to higher food consumption and significant food waste, including nutrient-rich by-products from fruits such as stems, rinds, peels, and seeds. Despite their valuable nutrients, these fruit by-products are often discarded. With growing interest in nutrient-dense foods, these by-products present an opportunity to be upcycled into functional ingredients. Upcycling involves repurposing food waste into useful products, offering a sustainable approach to reducing waste while enhancing nutritional content.\n\nWhite flour, widely used in food products like bread and pasta, possesses good functional properties but lacks sufficient nutritional value. Enhancing white flour by blending it with flours made from fruit by-products can create nutrient-rich, functional mixtures. This review specifically highlights the use of flours from common Brazilian fruit by-products, including jackfruit, among others such as jaboticaba, avocado, guava, mango, banana, orange, pineapple, and passion fruit. Incorporating jackfruit food product flours partially in wheat flour can increase fiber, protein, and carbohydrates, thus improving the flour's nutritional quality.\n\nHowever, higher amounts of substitution with jackfruit food product flour and other fruit by-product flours may alter the color and flavor of the final products, potentially affecting their sensory appeal and consumer acceptability. Despite the common perception of ASBs and fruit juices as better options, their consumption was associated with elevated cardiometabolic disease risks and mortality outcomes. The findings support caution in substituting SSBs with artificially sweetened or fruit juice beverages to achieve improved health outcomes.\n\nIn conclusion, higher consumption of both artificially sweetened beverages and fruit juices appears linked to increased cardiometabolic disease risk and mortality, challenging their use as healthier beverage alternatives to sugar-sweetened beverages. This summary discusses the case of a full-term male newborn diagnosed with Prune-Belly syndrome. At birth, clinical examination revealed typical signs of the syndrome including hypoplasia of the abdominal muscles, urinary tract dilatation, cryptorchidism, and renal failure. Diagnostic confirmation was achieved through physical assessment, abdominal ultrasonography, and blood tests measuring urea and creatinine levels, indicating compromised kidney function.\n\nManagement of Prune-Belly syndrome often requires a multidisciplinary approach. Early diagnosis of Prune-Belly syndrome is crucial to plan timely surgical correction and improve long-term outcomes. Unfortunately, in this case, the recommended surgical procedures could not be performed promptly, and the infant succumbed to kidney failure on the seventh day of life.\n\nThe prognosis for infants with Prune-Belly syndrome varies depending on the severity of urinary tract involvement and renal impairment. Quality antenatal monitoring plays a vital role in enhancing the outcome by facilitating early detection of Prune-Belly syndrome, thus allowing preparation for immediate postnatal care and surgical intervention. The only exception was MAB levels in the 4% NaCl/\u22122.41\u00b0C solution, which did not differ significantly from the control. Overall, the findings suggest that subzero saline chilling enhances carcass chilling efficiency and bacterial reduction without compromising the yield or cooking quality of turkey fillets. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/IAO_0000104": "This manuscript evaluates the representation of plan specification execution within the Open Biological and Biomedical Ontology (OBO) Foundry, focusing on the prevailing \u201cRC-account\u201d pattern. The RC-account models the execution of a plan specification as a process in which a realizable entity, termed a realizable concretization (RC), concretizes and is realized according to the plan specification. This approach straightforwardly links the plan specification to the entity bearing the RC and the process realizing it. However, the authors identify critical limitations in the RC-account regarding the representation of failed plans. Specifically, when the realizable concretization is flawed or the execution process fails to enact the actions outlined by the plan specification, the RC-account does not clearly define the nature of the relationship between the realizable entity and the plan specification. This ambiguity extends to how failed executions relate directly to entities carrying out instructions derived from the plan specification. The issues become more complex in contexts involving evolving or changing plans. To address these shortcomings, the manuscript proposes two solutions for representing failed plans involving plan specifications. The first, simpler solution employs the Common Core Ontologies\u2019 \u2018prescribed by\u2019 relation, linking the plan specification to the entity or process using it as a guiding framework. This method is hypothesized to be sufficient for most scenarios involving plan specifications. The second, more elaborate solution integrates the process of creating a plan, framed as an intention to execute the plan specification, into the representation, thereby enriching the modeling of plan specification execution and failure. The authors conclude that although the \u2018prescribed by\u2019 relation offers a practical and generally adequate approach, additional research is necessary to empirically validate this hypothesis and to further explore more complex representational frameworks for plan specification execution and failure. This work provides ontology developers with a critical assessment of current methods for modeling plan specifications and guidance on improving the representation of failed and changing plan executions.",

Traditional reliance on food crops for bioethanol production has caused environmental issues, prompting a shift toward non-food sources such as algal food material. Algae, rich in carbohydrates stored as food storage sugars and structural polysaccharides, offer a sustainable alternative for bioethanol production. The algal food storage polysaccharides primarily consist of glucose subunits but differ in their glycosidic bonds. Starch-type polysaccharides (e.g., starch, floridean starch, glycogen) feature \u03b1-(1\u21924) and \u03b1-(1\u21926) bonds, while laminarin-type polysaccharides (e.g., laminarin, chrysolaminarin, paramylon) contain \u03b2-(1\u21923) and \u03b2-(1\u21926) bonds. Structural polysaccharides in algal food material vary more widely in composition and bonding patterns.\n\nEfficient enzymatic hydrolysis and fermentation of these diverse algal food storage polysaccharides are critical for industrial bioethanol production. Compared to terrestrial plants, the enzymatic breakdown of algal polysaccharides requires more complex enzyme mixes due to their diverse structures. Additionally, algal fermentable sugars present a wider array of monosaccharides, necessitating varied metabolic pathways for ethanol production. Common yeast strains like Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Zymomonas mobilis can ferment glucose, galactose, and glucose isomers from algal food material by converting glucose through glycolysis via the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas or Entner-Doudoroff pathways. However, these microbes cannot ferment alginate, a significant component of algal food material. Ethanol production from alginate has thus been achieved through genetically engineered strains capable of both hydrolyzing and fermenting this polysaccharide.\n\nThis review highlights the enzymatic hydrolysis processes essential for breaking down different algal food storage polysaccharides and emphasizes the major metabolic pathways involved in fermenting various algal monosaccharides to ethanol. The diverse composition of algal food material necessitates advanced biotechnological approaches to optimize bioethanol yield from third-generation biomass sources.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/BFO_0000017": "This manuscript evaluates the use of the \u201crealizable concretization\u201d (RC) account within the Open Biological and Biomedical Ontology (OBO) Foundry framework, which represents the execution of a plan specification as a process involving a realizable entity that concretizes the plan specification. The RC-account connects the plan specification, the realizable entity bearing the realizable concretization, and the process realizing this concretization. While this approach offers a clear means to relate plans to their executions, its adequacy has not been systematically assessed until now.\n\nThe analysis reveals key limitations of the RC-account, particularly in handling failed plans. When a realizable entity\u2019s concretization is flawed, the relationship between the realizable entity and the original plan specification becomes ambiguous. Furthermore, if the execution of the realizable concretization fails to carry out the prescribed actions, the RC-account does not offer a clear way to directly link the failed execution to the entity implementing the plan. These deficiencies become even more problematic when plans change over time, complicating the representation of realizable entities involved in dynamic contexts.\n\nTo address these shortcomings, the authors propose two representational solutions for failed plans. The first employs the Common Core Ontologies\u2019 \u2018prescribed by\u2019 relation to connect the plan specification to the entity or process that uses the plan as a guide. This solution maintains the involvement of the realizable entity in a manner consistent with standard ontological relations and is hypothesized to be sufficient in most cases. The second, more nuanced solution integrates the process of creating a plan\u2014understood as an intention to execute a plan specification\u2014into the model of executing plan specifications, potentially providing a more comprehensive framework for representing realizable entities amidst plan failure or modification.\n\nIn conclusion, while the RC-account effectively relates realizable entities to plan execution under ideal conditions, its limitations in representing failed or evolving plans suggest the need for alternative approaches. The proposed solutions offer promising directions to improve how realizable entities and their associated plans are ontologically represented, inviting further research to validate and extend these frameworks.",

Importantly, incorporating the forest phase leads to an average increase of 5.98 cm in snow depth estimation within forest areas, effectively reducing the underestimation commonly observed in forests. Initial diagnosis relies on anteroposterior and lateral pelvis radiographs, although CT, MRI, and bone scans can provide increased sensitivity.\n\nThe vascular nature of the cancellous bone involved in comminuted IT fractures can result in significant blood loss and potential complications such as compartment syndrome. Given the complexity and instability associated with comminuted intertrochanteric fractures, early orthopedic consultation is critical. At 1.0 mM, l-ascorbyl palmitate had no significant impact on the oxidation rate or stability. However, at the highest tested concentration (2.0 mM), l-ascorbyl palmitate provided a pronounced antioxidant effect, substantially enhancing the oil\u2019s resistance to oxidation.\n\nAdditionally, the study compared the antioxidant activity of rosmarinic acid (0.2 mM) with l-ascorbyl palmitate. Rosmarinic acid alone improved camelina oil stability significantly. Yet, when combined with l-ascorbyl palmitate at a 1:1 ratio and the same concentration, the mixture\u2019s antioxidant efficacy was markedly diminished compared to rosmarinic acid alone. \n\nIn summary, l-ascorbyl palmitate has a complex, concentration-dependent role in modulating the oxidative stability of camelina seed oil. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03411090": "The computation of gas dispersal in urban or hilly areas typically demands significant computer resources when using conventional multidimensional models based on two-phase flow or Navier-Stokes equations. Simplified models, such as two-layer shallow water models, offer an attractive alternative for large-scale dispersion by performing 2D simulations that approximate 3D effects, thus significantly reducing CPU time. However, these models encounter three main challenges. The first is the lack of hyperbolicity in most existing formulations, which impacts wave propagation accuracy. The second challenge involves non-conservative terms in the momentum equations that represent interactions between fluid layers. These two difficulties were recently addressed in Chiapolino and Saurel (2018), where an unconditional hyperbolic model was introduced along with a Harten-Lax-van Leer (HLL) type Riemann solver designed to handle the non-conservative terms. Numerical experiments in that work demonstrated the robustness and accuracy of the proposed formulation by Saurel and colleagues. The current study focuses on the third challenge: determining an appropriate drag effect formulation between fluid layers, which is especially critical in heavy-gas dispersion scenarios. The model's drag force correlation, accounting for interactions between heavy and light gas layers, is validated against laboratory dam-break tests. Results confirm that the model, building on the foundation laid by Saurel\u2019s earlier work, accurately reproduces experimental observations. This progress emphasizes the significance of Saurel\u2019s contributions in addressing fundamental issues in two-layer shallow water modeling and in improving the simulation of heavy gas dispersal with computational efficiency and physical fidelity.",

Other traits, such as fresh curd yield and energy recovery in the sheep milk curd, showed moderate but still useful predictive performance for dairy processing monitoring. The leave-one-out validation revealed lower accuracies, attributed to differences among farming systems between calibration and validation sets. Including farm-related information could improve the prediction of sheep milk curd traits.\n\nSignificant predictive contributions originated from FTIR spectral regions related to \u201cwater\u201d and the \u201cfingerprint\u201d areas, emphasizing the importance of including water region data in modeling to maintain prediction accuracy for sheep milk curd traits. The squirrels\u2019 adaptive behavior of shaping and fitting tree nuts between twigs ensures more secure storage, increasing their food supply during dry periods within the humid tropical rainforest. Beyond benefiting the squirrels, this caching method also likely influences the spatial distribution and regeneration of tree species in the forest by dispersing tree nuts away from parent trees. In total, 139 isolates were obtained from the cornichon pickle fermentations.\n\nThroughout the study, salt, acidity, and pH levels of both the brine and cornichon pickles were regularly monitored. The isolates were tested for growth and gas production from glucose under varying conditions, including temperatures of 10\u00b0C, 45\u00b0C, and 50\u00b0C; salt concentrations of 2%, 4.5%, and 10% (w/w); and pH values of 3, 4.5, and 9.6. Eight isolates were identified as heterofermentative based on their ability to produce CO2 from glucose. Most isolates displayed optimal growth at 10\u00b0C, with very few growing at higher temperatures of 45\u00b0C and 50\u00b0C. No isolates were able to grow at pH 9.6, 25 grew at pH 4, and only 4 showed growth at pH 3. Salt tolerance varied, with only one isolate showing resistance to 10% salt, while almost all grew well at 2% and 6.5% salt concentrations.\n\nFurther identification of 48 selected isolates using API 50 CHL revealed that Lactobacillus pentosus and Lactobacillus plantarum were dominant throughout the cornichon pickle fermentations. Specifically, 19 isolates\u20148 from vinegar-based and 11 from AW-based cornichon pickles\u2014were L. pentosus, while 29 isolates\u201416 from vinegar and 13 from AW cornichon pickles\u2014were L. plantarum.\n\nIn conclusion, the microbial flora in cornichon pickles produced with vinegar and AW were similar, with L. plantarum and L. pentosus serving as the dominant lactic acid bacteria species. The results indicate that acid whey can be successfully used as an alternative brine medium for cornichon pickle production.",

Extensive independent studies have focused on these regulated processing events, including alternative splicing (AS) and alternative polyadenylation (APA). Emerging evidence highlights potential crosstalk between splicing and 3\u2032-end regulated processing aids in controlling AS and APA. This review first outlines the molecular machines involved in these regulated processing aids, then summarizes recent findings on the mechanisms and functions of their interplay.\n\nThe 3\u2032-end regulated processing aids not only promote the splicing of the last intron via factors and CPA-generated polyA tails but also influence splicing of internal and terminal exons. Additionally, the length of the 3\u2032 untranslated region (3\u2032 UTR), shaped by 3\u2032-end regulated processing aids, can modulate the splicing of upstream exons. Conversely, splicing and CPA can compete as regulated processing aids within introns to generate diverse RNA products. Splicing within the 3\u2032 UTR further contributes to its diversity, and certain splicing factors regulate 3\u2032-end processing, indicating their role as regulated processing aids.\n\nInterestingly, some classical RBPs serve dual roles in both splicing and 3\u2032-end regulated processing aids, underscoring the integrated nature of these processes. Advances in long-read sequencing technologies enhance understanding of the coordination between AS and APA as regulated processing aids. This knowledge of regulated processing aids offers promising avenues for novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies in disease contexts by targeting the coordination of AS-APA events.\n\nIn summary, the interplay of splicing and 3\u2032-end CPA as regulated processing aids reveals a complex regulatory network essential for RNA diversity and function, with significant potential impacts on biomedical research and clinical applications.",

Fe\u2010TA is not an irritant to skin or eyes, is not a skin sensitizer, and shows low acute dermal toxicity. Additionally, no environmental risks are expected from the use of Fe\u2010TA in salt for animal nutrition.\n\nThe FEEDAP Panel concludes that Fe\u2010TA has potential efficacy as an anticaking agent when incorporated into salt at the minimum proposed level of 3 mg iron per kg salt (equivalent to 26 mg Fe\u2010TA per kg salt on a dry matter basis). "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03311226": "This study focused on the moisture sorption isotherm and thermal characteristics of freeze-dried tuna to better understand factors influencing its stability. Water activity is a key factor in food stability, and the relationship between water activity and equilibrium moisture content (moisture sorption isotherm) aids in modeling drying processes and estimating shelf life. Additionally, glass transition temperatures provide insight into molecular mobility, which influences food stability. \n\nMoisture sorption isotherm measurements for freeze-dried tuna flesh were conducted at 20\u00b0C, and thermal characteristics were analyzed over a temperature range from -90 to 250\u00b0C using Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC). The moisture sorption data were modeled using the BET (Brunauer-Emmett-Teller) and GAB (Guggenheim-Anderson\u2013De Boer) models, yielding monolayer water values for freeze-dried tuna of 0.052 g/g dry solids (GAB) and 0.089 g/g dry solids (BET). \n\nDSC thermograms of freeze-dried tuna samples with moisture content above 0.10 g/g (wet basis) exhibited two-step state changes (two glass transitions), along with one exothermic peak attributed to molecular ordering and one endothermic peak corresponding to solids melting. In contrast, freeze-dried tuna samples with lower moisture content (0.046 g/g) showed three-step state changes (three glass transitions), which may reflect the natural heterogeneity of tuna flesh and molecular incompatibility among its components.\n\nThe first glass transition temperature and exothermic peak were not significantly affected by moisture content in freeze-dried tuna samples (p>0.05). However, the third glass transition temperature decreased with increasing moisture content, indicating plasticization (p<0.05). The solids-melting peak temperature of freeze-dried tuna decreased, and melting enthalpy increased as moisture content decreased (p<0.05).\n\nOverall, determination of the moisture sorption isotherm and thermal transitions in freeze-dried tuna provides critical information for identifying monolayer moisture and stable glassy states, which are essential for optimizing the storage stability and shelf life of freeze-dried tuna products.",

However, the benefits linked to red wine are partly due to its flavonoid content, suggesting that a diet rich in fruits and vegetables containing these compounds could provide even greater cardiovascular protection than red wine alone. Researchers measured survival, recovery, and key desiccation-related traits such as fresh mass, percentage water content, percentage cuticle content, and water loss rate under controlled desiccation conditions. The results indicated that meso- and hypersaline species, regardless of inhabiting lentic or lotic water bodies, were more resistant to desiccation, exhibiting significantly lower water loss rates and higher water content compared to freshwater and hyposaline species. Interestingly, no consistent patterns in desiccation resistance traits emerged between species from lotic and lentic water bodies. Within species, water loss rate correlated positively with initial percentage water content but showed no relation to fresh mass or cuticle content, suggesting that water loss dynamics primarily depend on the amount of body water available. These findings support earlier hypotheses that the evolution of desiccation resistance in aquatic beetles is linked to the colonization of saline habitats. Moreover, interspecific patterns observed in Enochrus beetles imply that freshwater species from both lotic and lentic water bodies may be more vulnerable to drought intensification predicted under climate change, especially in arid and semi-arid regions such as the Mediterranean Basin. Overall, this research enhances understanding of how desiccation resistance varies among species associated with lotic water bodies and highlights the potential risks freshwater beetles face in increasingly dry environments.",

"https://www.w3.org/TR/owl-time/#time:TemporalEntity": "Biomedical named entity recognition (Bio-NER) is essential for extracting knowledge from biomedical texts, where identifying temporal entities plays a critical role in understanding timing-related information. Current state-of-the-art Bio-NER models typically rely on bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) and bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT). Despite their effectiveness, these models require substantial computational resources. Addressing this challenge, the paper introduces a temporal convolutional network (TCN) combined with a conditional random field (CRF) layer, termed TCN-CRF, specifically applied to Bio-NER tasks involving temporal entity recognition. The TCN is adept at capturing sequential dependencies over time, which is particularly beneficial for accurately extracting temporal entities. In this model, TCNs are employed to extract relevant features from input sequences, which are subsequently decoded by the CRF layer to produce the final entity predictions, including temporal entities. Enhancements to the original TCN involve fusing features extracted by convolution kernels of varying sizes, further boosting the recognition of temporal entities within biomedical texts. The approach was evaluated on benchmark datasets such as GENIA and CoNLL-2003, both of which contain complex entity annotations including temporal entities relevant to biomedical and general named entity extraction. Experimental results demonstrate that the TCN-CRF model achieves performance comparable to five leading deep learning models while significantly reducing training time, emphasizing its efficiency in identifying temporal entities. To address this, the study evaluated improved cultivars of maize and cowpea for both food and feed purposes through intercropping trials using the \u201cmother and baby trials\u201d approach with crop\u2013livestock farmers. The mother trial featured a randomized block design with eight treatments and four replicates, involving two cowpea cultivars (KVx745-11P and Tiligr\u00e9) and two maize cultivars (Barka and Espoir), grown under monoculture and intercropping systems. Baby trials were conducted on-farm with 30 farmers across two seasons (2019 and 2020) in four villages of the South Sudan zone, Burkina Faso.\n\nData collected focused on weed density and biomass, grain yield and fodder biomass, intercropping efficiency, and fodder nutritive value. Statistical analysis showed that intercropping maize and cowpea significantly reduced weed biomass (p \u2264 0.05). In monoculture, maize cultivar Barka outperformed Espoir in both grain yield (4980 kg/ha vs. 2581 kg/ha) and fodder biomass (6259 kg DM/ha vs. 4952 kg DM/ha). The cowpea cultivars, KVx745-11P and Tiligr\u00e9, produced similar fodder biomass (2435\u20132820 kg DM/ha) and grain yield (1152\u20131163 kg/ha), indicating their reliability as sources of animal feed.\n\nIntercropping improved land equivalent ratios for both fodder biomass (1.18 to 1.41) and grain yield (1.02 to 1.44), showing greater efficiency compared to monoculture systems. The crude protein concentration in fodder was higher for cowpea KVx745-11P (19%\u201321.8%) than for cowpea Tiligr\u00e9 (15%\u201317%), highlighting the nutritional benefits of cowpea as animal feed. Maize cultivars had lower crude protein levels, with Barka (9.5%\u20139.8%) outperforming Espoir (8.5%\u20138.7%).\n\nOverall, intercropping maize, particularly the Barka cultivar, with cowpea KVx745-11P was the most effective system for maximizing grain yield and fodder biomass, providing quality cowpea fodder for animal feed and enhancing crop\u2013livestock farming productivity in Burkina Faso's South Sudan zone.",

Forests serve as a natural source of airborne summer bolete spores, with their sporulation timing, intensity, and dispersal influenced by land use and meteorological factors. The research aimed to analyze how summer bolete spore concentrations vary depending on land cover and weather conditions.\n\nUsing a volumetric method and spore traps placed at different heights and locations with varying land cover types, the study found that summer bolete spores occur in high concentrations during late summer and autumn. Regions with more green areas, including forests, showed higher concentrations of summer bolete spores.\n\nThe diurnal cycle analysis revealed two daily peaks in summer bolete spore concentration, particularly evident at ground level. Among the environmental variables assessed, air temperature and humidity were the primary weather factors impacting the presence of airborne summer bolete spores.\n\nThis research highlights that understanding the dynamics of summer bolete spore concentrations requires considering multiple environmental factors, including habitat characteristics, climate conditions, geobotany, and land use. Such comprehensive analysis is essential for accurately interpreting aeromycological phenomena related to summer bolete spores and other basidiospores.\n\nIn conclusion, the occurrence and dispersal of summer bolete spores are closely linked to land cover, especially forested areas, and meteorological conditions like temperature and humidity. LAL\u2019s unique sensitivity and specificity to gram-negative bacteria, which account for 70\u201380% of sepsis-causing pathogens, make it crucial in managing infectious diseases. Past efforts to apply LAL clinically were limited by interference from substances in blood, but the new LAL-based assay developed in this research overcomes such challenges by detecting gram-negative bacteria and endotoxins in human blood without interference, using aquaculture-derived LAL.\n\nIn summary, sustainable production of LAL as a key whelk material through HSC aquaculture can reduce dependence on wild populations, ensuring a steady and responsible supply. Institutional reviews reveal that many trials exclude non-English speakers, citing lack of resources or implicit bias. Recommendations include HHS publishing translated templates for common languages, creating a federal database of qualified translators, funding translation services, clarifying the witness role in the Common Rule, requiring IRBs to justify English fluency exclusions, and implementing cultural competency training.\n\nThe author concludes federal regulations lack specificity and enforcement, resulting in unequal research experiences and potential data bias. The study aimed to identify each stage of the granulated coconut sugar production process at the farmer level\u2014from collecting coconut sap to producing the granulated product\u2014and analyze its total environmental impact using the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) approach coupled with the CML-IA Baseline calculation method.\n\nThe research scope covered a \"gate-to-gate\" inventory of inputs and outputs, tracing every stage from sap heating to the final granulated coconut sugar, and interpreting the environmental impacts associated with each phase. The functional unit for analysis was 1 kg of farmer-produced granulated coconut sugar. The largest contributor to GWP was the use of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG), accounting for 2.89E-02 kg CO2 eq. In contrast, firewood use was the main driver of AP and EP impacts, contributing 8.16E-04 kg SO2 eq and 2.12E-04 kg PO4 eq respectively.\n\nAn improvement scenario was evaluated by substituting firewood with rice husks as the energy source in the granulated coconut sugar production process. For almond ash, the removal percentage declined from 78.93% to 37.01% over the same concentration range. Increasing the dose of almond green hull enhanced removal efficiency, eventually reaching nearly 100%. In contrast, increasing the almond ash dose initially increased chromium removal, but further increases led to a decline in efficiency.\n\nThe study concludes that both almond green hull and its resultant ash serve as effective agents for removing hexavalent chromium from contaminated water. Almond green hull exhibits superior performance compared to almond ash, particularly at varying chromium concentrations and adsorbent dosages. More recently, Beihang University\u2019s Lunar Palace 1 facility combined air, water, and food production for three humans within a 69 m\u00b2 agricultural module.\n\nThese space agriculture studies have yielded innovations\u2014such as LED lighting for crops, vertical farming techniques, hydroponic cultivation of subterranean crops, enhanced crop yields surpassing terrestrial records, and sophisticated water and waste recycling\u2014all supporting sustainable organic agriculture diets. The research highlights the northward migration of these zones, including the warm summer climatic zone, which is driven by gradual warming across Europe. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_00003214": "The text discusses the critical role of epicardial adipose tissue, often referred to as epicardial fat, in the link between obesity, type 2 diabetes, and atrial fibrillation (AF). Both obesity and diabetes cause expansion of epicardial fat, which releases proinflammatory adipocytokines contributing to microvascular dysfunction and fibrosis in the myocardium. When epicardial fat accumulation occurs adjacent to the left atrium, it leads to atrial myopathy manifesting clinically as AF. In patients with AF, epicardial fat volume closely correlates with the severity of electrophysiological abnormalities in neighboring myocardial tissue, and increased epicardial fat mass serves as a predictor of AF in the general population.\n\nThe expansion of epicardial fat in obesity and type 2 diabetes also impacts the left ventricle, impairing its distensibility and potentially causing heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Diagnosing HFpEF in patients with obesity or diabetes and AF can be challenging because dyspnea may be mistakenly attributed to body mass or arrhythmia. The effectiveness of treatments for obesity, diabetes, or AF is influenced by their impact on epicardial fat-related inflammation and the resulting atrial and ventricular myopathy.\n\nTherapeutic interventions such as bariatric surgery and metformin help reduce epicardial fat mass and improve AF outcomes. Conversely, insulin promotes adipogenesis and cardiac fibrosis, increasing the risk of AF. Rate control strategies for AF, which allow prolonged ventricular filling, may impair exercise tolerance in patients with cardiac fibrosis and HFpEF, who cannot tolerate volume loading. Additionally, both obesity and diabetes reduce the success of rhythm control strategies (e.g., electrical cardioversion, catheter ablation) for AF due to elevated epicardial fat volumes and associated cardiac fibrosis, which contribute to AF recurrence.\n\nIn summary, epicardial fat plays a central pathological role in the interplay among obesity, type 2 diabetes, and AF, affecting atrial and ventricular function, influencing treatment responses, and determining the prognosis of AF in affected patients.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_00003094": "Following a request from the European Commission, EFSA evaluated the safety and efficacy of star anise tincture, a product derived from the fruit (pericarps and seeds) of Illicium verum Hook f. (star anise), intended as a sensory feed additive for all animal species. The star anise tincture is a \u25a0\u25a0\u25a0\u25a0\u25a0 solution with approximately 1.86% dry matter. It contains on average 0.2588% polyphenols (including 0.0229% flavonoids and 0.0036% rutin), 0.018% anethole, and 0.00039% estragole.\n\nThe EFSA Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed (FEEDAP) concluded that star anise tincture is safe when added to complete feed at levels up to 200 mg/kg for horses and 50 mg/kg for all other animal species. The use of star anise tincture in drinking water is also considered safe, provided that total daily intake does not exceed amounts deemed safe through feed consumption.\n\nNo safety concerns for consumers are anticipated from the use of star anise tincture at the proposed feed levels. However, star anise tincture should be handled with caution, as it is identified as an irritant to skin and eyes and may act as a dermal and respiratory sensitiser. Exposure to estragole in the star anise tincture cannot be excluded during handling, so user exposure should be minimized to reduce risk.\n\nEnvironmental risks from using star anise tincture as a flavour additive in animal feed are not expected. Given that the fruit of Illicium verum and its preparations, including star anise tincture, are already recognized to provide flavour in food, and the intended function in feed is similar, no additional demonstration of efficacy was considered necessary.\n\nIn summary, star anise tincture is safe for animal species at specified levels in feed and water, poses no consumer or environmental risks, but requires precautions to protect users from potential irritant and sensitising effects.",

Additionally, the changes in these compounds during the ageing process are examined, alongside the identification of potential ageing markers that are important for ensuring the authenticity and quality of Madeira wine.\n\nAnalytical techniques such as gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), two-dimensional gas chromatography, and time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC\u00d7GC-ToFMS) are employed in conjunction with chemometric methods like partial least squares regression (PLS-R) and partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA). These approaches help establish reliable ageing markers for Madeira wine, supporting authenticity verification.\n\nAmong the chemical families linked most closely with the ageing of Madeira wine are acetals, furanic compounds, and lactones. These compounds are integral to the sensory and chemical evolution of Madeira wine during maturation, underpinning its distinctive character and exceptional quality. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_00002781": "This study investigates the bacterial communities associated with pigeon pea, a legume native to India and a vital protein source for over a billion people in developing countries. Pigeon pea forms symbioses with nitrogen-fixing (N2-fixing) bacteria, but poor nodulation in Indian agricultural soils is a persistent problem. The research focuses on how factors such as location relative to the plant roots, developmental stage, soil type, and pigeon pea genotype influence bacterial populations. The results reveal that root proximity is the key determinant of microbial community composition, followed by plant developmental stage and soil characteristics, while pigeon pea genotype has a minor effect.\n\nPigeon pea roots exhibit reduced microbial diversity compared to surrounding soil, selectively enriching Proteobacteria, particularly Rhizobium species, during vegetative growth. Native pigeon pea symbionts, notably Bradyrhizobium spp., are present but their abundance varies depending on pigeon pea variety and soil conditions. Through 16S rRNA gene amplicon surveys, bacterial strain isolation, and co-inoculation experiments, it was demonstrated that non-nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium spp. are more successful root colonizers than Bradyrhizobium, which are the true nodule-forming symbionts of pigeon pea. This competitive disadvantage may underlie poor nodulation in Indian soils.\n\nThe findings emphasize that selecting effective pigeon pea inoculant strains should consider not only nitrogen fixation efficiency but also the ability to successfully colonize roots amid competing microbes. Although efforts have sought optimal N2-fixing symbionts for pigeon pea, no broadly effective strains have emerged yet. Notably, the establishment of nitrogen-fixing symbiosis in pigeon pea appears decoupled from root colonization competitiveness.\n\nGiven pigeon pea\u2019s importance as a staple for low-income populations and its potential in sustainable, low-input agriculture, improving its symbiotic relationships with rhizobia could significantly enhance yield, reduce food insecurity, and decrease reliance on synthetic fertilizers. Therefore, targeting both the symbiotic effectiveness and colonization competitiveness of pigeon pea symbionts represents a promising path to increase this crop\u2019s productivity and global impact.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03304054": "Moderate electric fields (MEF) heating is an electro-assisted technology that uses alternating electrical current passed through food products, applying an electrical potential gradient up to 1000 V/cm with frequencies between 1 Hz and 10,000 Hz. This method dissipates heat directly inside the food, overcoming heat transfer limitations typical of conventional convection or conduction. Tomato-based hot sauces, including tomato sauce and variants such as tomato sauce with eggplant or minced meat, are globally popular dressing products. Traditionally, industrial heating processes for these tomato-based hot sauces employ hot water or steam as heat carriers, which can be inefficient and environmentally demanding. This study explores MEF heating as an innovative approach to enhance processing efficiency and reduce environmental impact in the production of tomato-based hot sauces. Three tomato-based hot sauce products were tested using a custom MEF system with applied electrical potential differences ranging from 50 V to 80 V. The even temperature distribution during MEF treatment allowed the use of a macroscopic transient energy balance model to estimate the electrical conductivity of the tomato-based hot sauces and its temperature dependence. Results revealed that the electrical conductivity of the tomato-based hot sauces ranged between 1 and 5 S/m, indicating strong susceptibility to MEF heating. These findings suggest that MEF technology can effectively and uniformly heat tomato-based hot sauces, potentially shortening production times and improving energy efficiency. Thus, MEF heating presents new opportunities for processing and preparing tomato-based hot sauces with enhanced sustainability and efficiency compared to traditional thermal methods.",
"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03490200": "This case report describes the successful lung resection of the right anterior segment in a 48-year-old woman who had undergone a left pneumonectomy two years prior. It also aids in understanding bone formation mechanisms, comparing different spinal fusion techniques, and studying the effects of pathological spinal structures. Nonetheless, as computational power and FEA software continue to improve, the accuracy and application scope of modeling spinal manufactured cages are expected to expand significantly.\n\nIn summary, FEA is crucial in the rapidly evolving field of spinal interbody cage development. It enables detailed quantitative and visual representation of the performance and characteristics of manufactured cages post-implantation. Addition of thermoplastic adhesive at the tube-to-tubesheet interface significantly enhances leakage resistance, improving leak path to nearly 100% remaining tubesheet thickness for 0.0 mm RC joints. Overall, while thermoplastic adhesive reinforcement can improve joint performance at tight clearances, its effectiveness diminishes or reverses at larger radial clearances, highlighting the critical interplay between adhesive application and joint geometry in thermoplastic hybrid systems. Key operating parameters controlling these steps include temperature, pressure, and residence time. Based on a challenge test, it was demonstrated that the recycling process can ensure the migration level of potential unknown contaminants into food remains below a conservatively modelled migration threshold of 0.1 \u03bcg/kg food.\n\nConsequently, the Panel concluded that the recycled PET obtained from this process does not raise safety concerns when used at up to 100% for manufacturing materials and articles intended for contact with all types of foodstuffs, including drinking water. This applies to long-term storage at room temperature or below, with or without hotfill conditions. The Panels\u2019 safety assessment includes the use of the washed PET flakes in contexts where food contact is involved, ensuring the safety of the final articles made from this recycled PET.\n\nHowever, these final articles are not intended for use in microwave or conventional ovens, and such uses fall outside the scope of this evaluation. Overall, the process involving washed PET flakes is supported by the Panel as safe for producing food contact materials under the described conditions.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03303225": "Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is a hereditary metabolic disorder affecting the breakdown of branched-chain amino acids due to a deficiency in the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKD) complex. This deficiency impairs the catabolism of amino acids such as leucine, isoleucine, and valine, leading to the accumulation of branched-chain amino acids as well as their corresponding alpha-keto acids and alpha-hydroxy acids in the blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid. The accumulation results in neurological damage and mental retardation if left untreated. MSUD is linked to mutations in genes encoding four subunits of the BCKD complex: BCKDHA, BCKDHB, DBT, and DLD.\n\nThis case report presents findings from three families whose newborn children exhibited symptomatic features of maple syrup urine disease in the first week after birth. Diagnosis was made using mass spectrometry to detect elevated branched-chain metabolites typically associated with maple syrup urine disease. Genetic analysis focusing on the four BCKD subunit genes confirmed disease-causing mutations.\n\nThe study identified a novel homozygous mutation, c.143delT, p.L48Rfs*15, in the BCKDHA gene responsible for the classic presentation of maple syrup urine disease. This mutation contributes to the defective function of the BCKD complex, causing the characteristic biochemical and clinical features of the disorder.\n\nEarly diagnosis through neonatal screening and DNA analysis is emphasized as critical for timely intervention and effective treatment of maple syrup urine disease. Recognizing the disease early can prevent the severe neurological complications associated with untreated maple syrup urine disease. The presence of the term \"syrup\" in the disease name highlights the characteristic sweet odor in affected patients' urine, a key clinical marker that aids in early suspicion and diagnosis.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03411025": "The bacterium Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii (Pss) causes Stewart\u2019s wilt disease in maize by forming biofilms in the xylem that block water transport, leading to wilting and necrosis. Infection initiates when the corn flea beetle vector introduces Pss into maize leaves, where the bacterium first colonizes the apoplast and subsequently moves to the xylem. A previous transposon sequencing (Tn-Seq) study identified essential genes for Pss survival in planta, including lrp, which encodes the global transcription factor leucine-responsive regulatory protein (Lrp). The Lrp protein is part of a widely distributed family found in many bacteria and archaea, where it regulates key physiological functions.\n\nIn Pss, Lrp positively controls traits crucial for virulence, such as motility and capsule production. This study employed RNA-Seq data analysis to define the Pss Lrp regulon by comparing gene expression between wild-type and \u2206lrp mutant strains grown in planta. Results revealed that Lrp regulates genes involved in capsule biosynthesis and nitrogen assimilation and metabolism. While the FEA results still underestimated in-plane deformation, they showed general improvement compared to previous models.\n\nThree key discrepancies were identified between experimental results and FEA predictions for paperboard container panels. First, the panels exhibited an initial region of low stiffness absent in FEA results, likely caused by imperfections in both the panels and test jig. Second, experimental stiffness was lower than that predicted by FEA; introducing an initial imperfection shaped like the first buckling mode into the model reduced the predicted stiffness, better aligning it with experiments. Third, panels displayed a stiffness reduction near failure not captured by the linear FEA model. To address this, a bi-linear material model was tested, showing potential to improve simulation accuracy.\n\nFurther testing involved box compression tests on a Regular Slotted Container (RSC) paperboard container with dimensions matching the tested panels. The paperboard container exhibited significantly greater displacement (13.1 mm) compared to the panel (3.5 mm), with an extended initial low-stiffness region corresponding to 7 mm displacement versus 0.5 mm for the panels. This highlights that complexities inherent to paperboard containers, such as horizontal creases, must be incorporated into finite element models for accurate prediction of in-plane deformation.\n\nIn summary, accurately modeling paperboard containers requires accounting for initial imperfections, material non-linearity (e.g., bi-linear material models), and structural complexities like creases. Incorporating these factors into FEA can enhance prediction of paperboard container behavior under compression, making simulations more representative of real-world performance.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_02010074": "The development and registration of veterinary medicinal products require extensive research beyond what is typically published in peer-reviewed journals. Registration dossiers include comprehensive data on product quality, safety, and efficacy, all evaluated by regulatory assessors with access to raw data. Studies must follow international standards such as Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP), Good Laboratory Practice (GLP), and Good Clinical Practice (GCP), with detailed protocols and validated measurement methods.\n\nAmong the critical components are target animal safety (TAS) studies, which assess the safety profile of the product using healthy experimental animals of the target species, typically involving multiple doses including multiples of the therapeutic dose. These studies focus on detecting effects on organ structure and function through clinical pathology (e.g., haematology, serum biochemistry) and detailed pathology examinations (both gross and histopathology), essentially examining various pieces of animal organ tissues for toxicological evaluation. While not powered to detect statistically significant differences, TAS studies are vital for identifying dose- or time-related adverse effects and informing the risk-benefit analysis.\n\nFurther safety assessment takes into account preclinical studies, including receptor binding, metabolism, mutagenicity, and data from human analogues when available. Post-authorisation pharmacovigilance relies on veterinary professionals reporting adverse effects observed in clinical use to continuously monitor safety.\n\nPublished studies in journals provide only a summary of the data due to manuscript limitations, omitting many ancillary studies and raw data critical to comprehensive safety assessments. Therefore, while pivotal field safety and efficacy (FSE) and TAS studies are key pieces of evidence involving animal tissues and organ evaluations, they represent only a portion of the full safety dossier required by regulatory authorities.\n\nIn summary, the safety evaluation of veterinary products heavily depends on detailed examinations of pieces of animal organ through pathology and clinical pathology, integrated with broad data sets to ensure a thorough risk-benefit assessment prior to and after product authorisation.",

The study found that the transmission of the eggshell is closely correlated with albumen changes during pickling. Specifically, transmittance exhibits an exponential decay over time, with the decay rate reflecting the pickling progress. Notably, during the initial phase, the colors of both albumen and yolk remain largely unchanged, similar to observations in chicken egg (pickled) processes. Importantly, this approach does not rely on progressive changes in light transmittance, offering a robust method for quality control. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03413384": "This study investigates the metabolic and lipidomic responses of Kentucky bluegrass to cadmium (Cd) stress, aiming to understand the mechanisms underlying its notable Cd tolerance and accumulation capacity. Soil Cd contamination is a serious environmental problem, and Kentucky bluegrass is recognized as a potential phytoremediator due to its resilience to Cd toxicity. However, the detailed metabolic pathways involved in Cd detoxification in Kentucky bluegrass remain unclear.\n\nUsing widely targeted metabolomics, the study compared Cd-resistant (M) and sensitive (R) varieties of Kentucky bluegrass to identify key metabolites involved in Cd stress response. The Cd-resistant Kentucky bluegrass variety (M) showed increased levels of free amino acids, saccharides, and diverse flavonoids\u2014including flavones, flavonols, isoflavones, and flavanones\u2014after Cd exposure, suggesting that these compounds play a role in enhancing Cd tolerance in the bluegrass plant.\n\nLipidomics analysis further revealed changes in the lipid profiles of Kentucky bluegrass under Cd stress. In the M variety, 183 lipid species (81%) decreased in abundance following Cd treatment, a considerably larger number compared to 81 lipid species (41.54%) showing similar reductions in the R variety. Among the lipid species whose abundance increased in Kentucky bluegrass were diacylglycerols, monogalactosyldiacylglycerol, phosphatidylcholine, triacylglycerol, and lysophosphatidylcholine, all exhibiting higher saturation levels. Conversely, lipid species with shorter acyl chains and higher unsaturation\u2014such as free fatty acids, phosphatidic acid, lysophosphatidic acid, phosphatidylglycerol, and others\u2014decreased in Kentucky bluegrass.\n\nThese lipidomic shifts in Kentucky bluegrass contribute to elongation of lipid acyl chains, leading to increased membrane thickness and rigidity through denser hydrophobic tail packing and augmented lipid-lipid interactions. This membrane modulation likely enhances Cd tolerance by affecting Cd distribution and accumulation in the bluegrass plant.\n\nIn summary, this study provides a comprehensive metabolite and lipid profile of Kentucky bluegrass under Cd stress, highlighting key metabolic and lipid homeostasis changes that support Cd detoxification and tolerance. These findings offer valuable insights into the metabolic regulation mechanisms in Kentucky bluegrass critical for improving phytoremediation strategies of Cd-contaminated soils.",

"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_00004200": "\u00a9 2009 by taylor & francis group, llc.the increase in the demand, and thus, in the export of tropical crops, have increased the need to investigate and to develop technologies that can maintain the quality and postharvest life of these crops for prolonged periods. modified atmosphere (ma) and controlled atmosphere (ca) are adequate technologies that can help extend the postharvest life of these crops. ma and ca are not used for storage of tropical crops, but are used for their marine transport (yahia, 1998a, 2006a). until recently many tropical fruits were only grown in home gardens and small farms primarily for local consumption. currently several tropical fruits are among the most important horticultural crops of international trade. the market for tropical fruits has increased significantly in the last few decades. this is due to several factors including changes in diet habits, demand for exotic articles, improved technologies such as storage and transport, and free under world trade organization (wto) regime. prices of agricultural commodities have been steadily declining in the last 20 years, however, tropical fruit prices have been rising (buchanan, 1994). the improved prices, improved technologies, and increased demand are resulting in increased plantations of a diversity of tropical fruits in several regions of the world. tropical crops are chilling sensitive (yahia, 2006b). some types of avocados, bananas, breadfruit, carambola, cherimoya, jackfruit, mamey, mango, mangosteen, papaya, pineapple, sapota, soursop, and white sapote are very sensitive to chilling injury (ci). durian, feijoa, sugar apple, and tamarillo are moderately sensitive. chilling sensitivity of tropical fruits does not permit their long-termmaintenance in low temperature, and as a consequence all these crops have a relatively short postharvest life compared to many temperate and subtropical fruits, only few weeks at the most. ma and ca have been shown to ameliorate chilling sensitivity in several crops, including those of tropical origin (yahia, 1998a, 2006b). the tropics are characterized by conditions that favor the spread of insects and diseases (high temperature and relative humidity). some of the most important diseases, which infect tropical fruits and cause major losses, include anthracnose (caused by colletotrichum gloeosprioides penz.) and stem end rot (caused by diplodia natalensis p. evans). anthracnose is the major postharvest problem in bananas, mangoes, papayas, and contributes to most of their losses. ma=ca can control some decay either directly or indirectly by delaying ripening and senescence of the commodity, and thus maintaining the resistance to pathogen attack (yahia, 1998a, 2006b). effective control of pathogens is essential for the postharvest maintenance of these crops, and for the successful application of ma=ca. many insects infect tropical fruit crops and impede their commercialization due to quarantine restrictions imposed by various countries (yahia, 1998b, 2004, 2006a). some of the most important insects include various species of fruit flies such as the ceratitis in several regions of the world, several anastrefa species in south and central america and the west indies, the genus dacus in africa and asia, etc. (yahia, 2006a). quarantine treatments for tropical fruits are needed in order to distribute them around the world. traditionally, chemical fumigants (mainly ethylene dibromide [edb]=and methyl bromide [mb]) have been the principal treatments used for this purpose. however, edb has been banned (federal register, 1984) because of health risks. mb is still been used for some crops, but with restrictions due to concerns over the use of toxic chemicals, and the uncertainty of prohibition. several physical treatments have been tried for quarantine purposes (yahia and ariza, 2001; yahia et al., 2004). low temperatures (08c-2.28c for 10-16 days) can be used for control of the mediterranean fruit fly. however, these temperatures cannot be used for most tropical fruits because of chilling sensitivity. hot water treatments (hwts) are been used in several countries to control fruit flies in mangoes (46.18c for 65-90min) and have been used in papaya (two-stage heating process with temperatures of 42 for 30min and 498c for 20min) (yahia, 2006a). vapor heat treatments have been developed and used (fons, 1990). injury have been reported in both mango and papaya fruits treated with heat (paull and armstrong, 1994). irradiation has proved potentially applicable for insect control in some tropical fruits such as mango and papaya (paull and armstrong, 1994; yahia, 2006a), however, commercial application is still very limited due to several problems including possible injury to the fruit, high costs, and consumer concerns. ma and ca (1.0 kpa o2 and=or 50 kpa co2) have insecticidal and fungistatic effects, and the potential to be developed as quarantine treatments as a safe alternative to the health-hazardous fumigants (yahia, 1998a, b; 2006a). for more details, see chapter 11. despite all the previously mentioned problems encountered for tropical fruit in post- harvest (chilling sensitivity, disease and insect infestations, and short postharvest life), tropical fruits need to be shipped to markets far away from growing areas, usually by air or sea. shipping by sea can take a very long time, but is economical compared to air-freight. for example, the minimum time required for sea freight from eastern australia to south east asia, japan and north america, and europe are 3, 4, and 6 weeks, respectively (mcglasson, 1989). minimum shipping periods from mexico to europe and japan are about 18 and 21 days, respectively (yahia, 1993a, 1995c). therefore, it is essential to assure a sufficiently long postharvest life for these crops to be able to be distributed in distant markets. in addition to better postharvest handling systems, which include optimum harvesting time, control of insects and diseases, and the use of ideal postharvest temperature management, ma and ca can be of major benefits to preserve the quality of these fruits and to prolong their postharvest life. the rising importance of tropical fruits in world trade and the recent developments in ma and ca technology and applications require the review of published research in order to suggest some valid conclusions and recommendations to improve the handling of tropical fruits, and in particular to increase the use of ma and ca. several excellent books and reviews have been written on ma and ca (dewey et al., 1969; dewey, 1977; smock, 1979; el-goorani and sommer, 1981; richardson and meheriuk, 1982; blankenship, 1985; kader, 1986; fellman, 1989; calderon and barkai-golan, 1990; blanpied, 1993). however, these covered mainly temperate (especially pome) fruits. very little research has been done on ma=ca of tropical crops as compared to temperate crops such as apples, pears, and kiwifruit. for example, out of 1982 articles published on ma=ca of fruits and vegetables from 1977 to 1993 <6% were on tropical fruits and vegetables (kader and morris, 1981, 1997; kader, 1985; zagory and kader, 1989, 1993). very few reviews have been written on ma=ca of tropical fruits (hatton and spalding, 1990; kader, 1993; yahia and paull, 1997; yahia, 1998a; yahia, 2006c), and information has been largely limited to mangoes, bananas, pineapples, and papayas. information on many of the minor tropical crops is either missing or dispersed in nonestablished journals and local reports.",

The research also highlights the crucial role of non-immune cells, notably epithelial cells, in orchestrating immune maturation within the sheep stomach. Cell communication analysis further indicates that, besides immune cells, non-immune cells in the forestomachs recruit immune cells through macrophage migration inhibitory factor signaling. Overall, this work demonstrates rapid immune and defense response development in all four sheep stomach chambers during the early postnatal period. It provides valuable insights into the gene expression patterns and cellular contributors underlying immune development in the sheep stomach. Additionally, the identification of key receptors and signaling pathways involved in immune regulation within the sheep stomach offers potential targets for nutritional and health management strategies to improve lamb health. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_02020839": "The text discusses the growing interest in metallic fuels for future sodium fast reactors, primarily due to their favorable material properties such as high thermal conductivity and beneficial neutronic characteristics, which enable greater fission densities. A key challenge with typical metallic fuels is zirconium (Zr) redistribution, which negatively affects the fuel's advantageous material and neutronic properties. Understanding the zirconium migration processes is complex and currently relies on first-principles knowledge, necessitating extensive characterization and fuel qualification before these fuels can be employed in reactors.\n\nTo support these activities, robust modeling tools like BISON are used to simulate the coupled thermo-mechanical behavior and nuclear properties of metallic fuels. BISON relies on empirical model parameters that must be validated against post-irradiation examination (PIE) measurements to ensure accurate simulations. The current study uses data from two fuel pins of the EBR-II experiment X441 to optimize BISON model parameters, including the porosity correction factor, thermal conductivity, phase transition temperature, and diffusion coefficient multipliers. Following this optimization, the finalized model is applied to seven fuel pins with varying characteristics.\n\nThe evaluation of BISON simulations is performed by comparing results to PIE metallography data to verify accurate representation of zirconium redistribution. Encouragingly, six out of seven fuel pins show good agreement between metallography images and BISON outputs, particularly in the alignment of Zr-rich, Zr-depleted, and moderately Zr-enriched zones along axial positions of the fuel pins. This demonstrates the effectiveness of BISON in modeling the complex zirconium migration in metallic fuels. Nonetheless, additional work remains to refine BISON model parameters to enhance its general applicability across different fuel pins.\n\nIn summary, BISON material modeling is a vital tool enabling the understanding and prediction of zirconium redistribution phenomena in metallic fuels, supporting the qualification and implementation of these fuels in future sodium fast reactors.",

The research evaluated the impact of different analysis pipelines, including high-quality single nucleotide polymorphism (hqSNP) pipelines and core/genome-wide multilocus sequence typing (cg/wgMLST) pipelines, as well as the choice of reference genomes on resulting data and interpretations.\n\nWGS data were generated from 40 Listeria monocytogenes isolates collected over 18 years from a cold-smoked salmon facility, a relevant food (cut) source, alongside two additional isolates from other facilities. Three hqSNP pipelines and two MLST pipelines analyzed the data. Initial clustering employed a k-mer approach, followed by hqSNP analyses using either closely related closed genomes (\u201cclosed references\u201d) or high-quality de novo draft assemblies from the dataset isolates (\u201cdraft references\u201d).\n\nResults demonstrated that all hqSNP pipelines yielded comparable hqSNP difference ranges among isolate clusters, with minimal impact from the type of reference genome used. Allelic differences from wgMLST were similar to hqSNP differences, while cgMLST consistently showed fewer differences. Phylogenetic trees based on hqSNP and cg/wgMLST data showed some incongruences, mainly involving clades with low bootstrap support.\n\nWhen applying an hqSNP cutoff to classify isolates as related or unrelated, different pipelines produced a significant number of discordances, emphasizing that cutoff values in food (cut)-related pathogen analyses should be a preliminary guide rather than definitive. Epidemiological context remains crucial for interpreting WGS data accurately.\n\nOverall, the study suggests cgMLST analyses offer effective subtype differentiation for food (cut)-associated pathogen isolates without the need for preliminary k-mer clustering or external closed references, simplifying workflows. Subsequent hqSNP or wgMLST analyses within cgMLST-defined clusters can enhance precision in assessing genomic similarity, benefiting food (cut) safety investigations and outbreak source tracking.",

The benefits of swell drying are attributed to its ability to prevent shrinkage and structural collapse of dried chokecherry tissues, thus enhancing the extraction of antioxidants.\n\nOverall, the study highlights swell drying as a promising technique to better preserve the valuable bioactive molecules in chokecherry compared to traditional methods, potentially reducing waste and improving the nutritional quality of preserved chokecherry products.",

Most body part weights, including pheasant carcass components, were unaffected by castration except for heart weight, which was notably higher in intact pheasants (P<0.05). The study concluded that castration tended to enhance growth performance predominantly within the initial 24 weeks of the fattening period, after which extended fattening was deemed impractical. A key distinguishing feature of the castrated pheasant carcass was the increased fat content in the meat. The authors suggest that further research under varied feeding and breeding systems is necessary to optimize pheasant carcass production. Originating throughout the Late Pleistocene, the Ice Complex not only preserves an archive of paleoenvironmental proxies such as Pleistocene faunal remains but also contains a record of human habitation dating back approximately 50,000 years, beginning with early MIS3. The development of syngenetic permafrost is crucial in shaping archaeological contexts in these ice-associated depositional settings.\n\nExcavations at the Yana site complex along the lower Yana River have offered a valuable opportunity to study archaeological finds preserved within Ice Complex deposits. Long-term field observations and dating efforts have led to significant geological conclusions regarding these Ice Complex sites. The thawing of frozen primary Ice Complex deposits has distorted original depositional sequences, generating secondary features like ice-wedge casts. Furthermore, collapsed blocks of frozen sediment, containing undisturbed frozen layers with artifacts or paleobiotic remains, may become refrozen into new depositional sequences, potentially causing misinterpretations and chronometric errors.\n\nSevere cryoturbation within polygonal mounds impacts sediment in contact with ice wedges, uplifting sediment contents and presenting several implications: (1) the true hypsometric provenience of datable material is altered, complicating dating accuracy; (2) archaeological interpretations of dating, cultural classification, and human behavior risk being skewed; (3) transported material can create secondary material concentrations at varied hypsometric levels, further complicating analysis; (4) in geology, the movement of geochemical signatures can lead to erroneous assessments of the area's geological potential; (5) uplifted deposits contribute to increased thickness of the Ice Complex, meaning its thickness reflects not only sedimentation but also sediment redistribution within preexisting polygon deposits.\n\nOverall, investigations of Ice Complex deposits at the Yana site have important broader implications for understanding Quaternary science, emphasizing the dynamic interactions between ice, sedimentation, and archaeological preservation.",
