"http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_03411140": "Empty fruit bunch (EFB), a significant by-product of the fruit-producing plant palm oil industry, represents a substantial and previously underutilized renewable energy resource for many countries in South East Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. This study focuses on the design and simulation of a plant that produces pure hydrogen through autothermal reforming (ATR) of palm empty fruit bunch (PEFB) derived from this fruit-producing plant. The process development was guided by successful laboratory experiments involving the core ATR stage.\n\nIn these experiments, the bio-oil feed to the ATR reactor, obtained from the fruit-producing plant\u2019s PEFB, was represented by a surrogate mixture comprising 11 organic compounds. These compounds are known main constituents of the real PEFB bio-oil based on previous research, selected to closely match its elemental composition and volatility. The experimental results demonstrated that hydrogen yields near equilibrium predictions are achievable by using an in-house synthesized Rh-Al\u2082O\u2083 catalyst within a packed bed reactor.\n\nSensitivity analysis of the plant design identified that the feed molar steam-to-carbon ratio should not exceed 3 for optimal hydrogen production efficiency in the ATR plant fueled by biomass from this fruit-producing plant. Initially, the overall plant efficiency was calculated at 39.4%, but this was significantly improved to 67.5% through the application of pinch analysis, which enhanced heat integration within the system.\n\nMoreover, the proposed hydrogen production plant utilizing biomass waste from the fruit-producing plant offers environmental benefits, with estimated CO\u2082 savings of approximately 0.56 kg per kilogram of raw PEFB processed. Together, the experimental studies and process design strongly support the potential for polygeneration of hydrogen, heat, and power from this otherwise discarded agricultural waste originating from the fruit-producing plant palm oil sector. This approach not only valorizes the waste from the fruit-producing plant but also contributes to sustainable energy development in tropical regions.\n\nIn summary, leveraging the fruit-producing plant by-product PEFB for ATR-based hydrogen production presents a promising and efficient renewable energy pathway with significant environmental and energy benefits.",

This study analyzes the mentions of N-a-s-i-r K-h-u-s-r-a-w in Iranian sources from after his death until 1000 AH, using a descriptive-analytical method, revealing three main approaches.\n\nFirst, the h-o-s-t-i-l-e approach appears mainly in Islamic sectology texts like MELAL WA NEHAL, where N-a-s-i-r K-h-u-s-r-a-w is called misguided and cursed (e.g., Hosseini Alavi, 1997; Fakhr Razi, 1992; Shabestri, 1991). Third, the l-e-g-e-n-d-a-r-y approach is dominant, attributing supernatural powers and mystical qualities to N-a-s-i-r K-h-u-s-r-a-w, making him a saintly figure in many sources. This includes fantastical stories from Qazvini\u2019s \"Asar al-Bilad\" of mysterious buildings and secret doors, as well as associations with personalities like Khayyam and Abul Hasan Kharqani (Rashidi, 1985; Dawlatshah Samarqandi, 2003). SCLEO demonstrated strong, dose-dependent antifungal activity by altering the mycelial morphology, cellular ultrastructure, and membrane permeability of B. cinerea, as observed under scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and fluorescence microscopy. This tapeworm is morphologically similar to but genetically distinct from D. latum and utilizes anadromous wild Pacific salmon as its second intermediate host. Infection in humans typically results in clinical symptoms such as diarrhea and discharge of the strobila, which can reach lengths up to 12 meters. While the natural life history and geographic range of D. nihonkaiense remain unclear, recent research suggests that brown bears along the northern Pacific coast serve as its natural final host. The increasing number of cases reflects a shift in the epidemiology of this tapeworm disease from predominantly rural populations to urban populations worldwide, largely linked to the consumption of seafood, including raw Pacific salmon, as part of a healthy diet. "http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/FOODON_00002373": "This study investigated postprandial glycemia (PPG) variability in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) not receiving insulin, focusing on the effects of meal times and food types. Using flash glucose monitoring (FGM) with the FreeStyle Libre system, 17 patients completed 153 food loading tests involving three types of food: boiled buckwheat (250 g), apple (200 g), and white bread (30 g), administered during breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Postprandial glucose was assessed by calculating the area under the glycemic curve (AUC) and delta AUC (area under curve excluding starting glycemia).\n\nThe study found that both food type and time of food intake significantly influenced the total glycemic response (AUC). Specifically, maximum AUC values were observed after breakfast compared to lunch and dinner (p=0.005 vs supper, p<0.001 vs dinner). Among the food types, buckwheat produced a higher AUC than apple (p=0.01). For the delta AUC, only food type had a significant effect (p=0.003), with buckwheat causing a greater rise in glucose compared to apple (p=0.001) and white bread (p=0.012).\n\nThese findings contrast with existing literature on individuals without T2DM, where postprandial glycemic peaks are typically highest after dinner. In this cohort of T2DM patients managed without insulin, the highest overall glucose response occurred after breakfast regardless of the type of food consumed. However, the relative rise in glucose (delta AUC) following a food load did not significantly differ by meal time, suggesting that time of food intake may not substantially alter glucose excursions relative to baseline in this group.\n\nIn conclusion, the study highlights that in T2DM patients not on insulin, postprandial glycemia is elevated most after breakfast compared to lunch and dinner, independent of food type. Buckwheat consistently elicited a stronger glycemic response than apple or white bread across meals. These results challenge the notion that dinner induces the highest postprandial glucose rises and emphasize the need to consider breakfast glycemic control in T2DM management.",

Applying a Bayesian modeling approach, researchers estimated the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves for each test, the true BTB prevalence among the Chadian cattle sample, and the disease status of individual animals without prior knowledge of their infection status.\n\nResults specific to the Chadian context showed that the SICCT test performed optimally when the positive cut-off was reduced to >2 mm from the standard >4 mm recommended by the OIE. At this cut-off, the SICCT test exhibited a sensitivity of 66% and specificity of 89%. In contrast, both FPA tests had sensitivities below 50%, though specificities exceeded 90%. The true BTB prevalence in the Chadian cattle population was estimated at 8%. Notably, 11% of animals showed gross tuberculous lesions on meat inspection; however, Bayesian analysis suggested that 72% of these lesions were caused by pathogens other than Mycobacterium bovis.\n\nThis study provides valuable insights into BTB diagnosis in a high-incidence sub-Saharan African setting, emphasizing the importance of locally adapted diagnostic thresholds. The Chadian results underline that lowering the SICCT test cut-off improves detection accuracy. Moreover, the application of Bayesian modeling offers a practical framework to evaluate diagnostic tests without gold standard reference data. Overall, the findings have significant implications for BTB control in Chad and similar contexts, enhancing the reliability of diagnosis and informing surveillance strategies.",

"https://www.w3.org/TR/owl-time/#time:Interval": "This study investigated the effects of interval training under hypoxia (IHT) on hematological parameters, hemodynamic function, and endurance exercise performance in amateur Korean female runners over a 6-week period. Twenty participants were equally divided into a normoxic training group (NTG) performing time interval training at normoxia (760 mmHg) and a hypoxic training group (HTG) performing time interval training under hypobaric hypoxia (526 mmHg, simulating 3000 m altitude). Both groups engaged in 120-minute training sessions three times per week, consisting of a 20-minute warm-up, 60 minutes of time interval training (10 repetitions of 5 minutes at 90\u201395% maximal heart rate (HRmax) followed by 1 minute rest), and a 20-minute cool-down.\n\nFollowing the intervention, significant increases in erythropoietin (EPO) levels were observed in both groups, with a more pronounced rise in the HTG. Time interval training under hypoxia led to decreased monocyte abundance, increased hematocrit and neutrophil counts, and decreased lymphocyte counts; conversely, the NTG exhibited increased B cell abundance. Both groups showed significant improvements in hemodynamic parameters, with the HTG displaying greater enhancements in oxygen uptake, stroke volume index, and end-diastolic volume index. Improvements in heart rate, end-systolic volume index, and cardiac output index were noted in both groups following time interval training.\n\nEndurance exercise performance, measured by maximal oxygen uptake and a 3000 m time trial, improved significantly in both groups, with the HTG tending to achieve greater performance gains. Importantly, hematological markers related to the immune system remained within normal ranges throughout the training period, indicating no negative impact from the time interval training under hypoxia.\n\nIn conclusion, 6 weeks of time interval training under hypoxia effectively enhanced endurance performance primarily through improved hemodynamic function, while maintaining stable hematological immune parameters. This supports the use of time interval IHT as a safe and efficient method to boost endurance capacity in amateur female runners.",

Genotoxicity data on polyglycerol esters of fatty acids are limited but do not indicate genotoxic potential. Reproductive toxicity studies on polyglycerol esters of fatty acids showed no adverse effects, although these studies had significant limitations.\n\nA clinical study involving volunteers receiving up to 300 mg/kg bw per day of polyglycerol esters of fatty acids for three weeks showed no adverse clinical chemistry or urinalysis findings, despite limited available information. Traditionally, classification within this neogastropod family has relied heavily on shell and radula morphology, with family membership typically confirmed by the unique radula structure characteristic of these neogastropods.
